# Pelican documentation

Every page of https://pelican.dev/docs/ as Markdown, in sidebar order. Pelican version 1.0.0-rc.4. Index: https://pelican.dev/llms.txt

# Welcome to Pelican!

> Introduction to the Pelican Panel and Wings, the service that runs game servers in Docker containers, with a glossary and an example setup.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/

This is the documentation for Pelican: how to install, update and run the Panel and Wings, set up webservers, SSL and eggs, and move over from Pterodactyl.

## What is Pelican?

[**Pelican**](https://github.com/pelican/panel) is a free, open-source server management panel for hosting game servers, software and applications in isolated Docker containers.
It started as a fork of [**Pterodactyl**](https://pterodactyl.io/) and has since grown well beyond it.

The Panel is the web interface: it shows information about your servers and sends commands to them.

## What is Wings?

[**Wings**](https://github.com/pelican/wings) is the service that runs on each machine hosting your servers.
It handles the Docker containers behind the scenes (creating, starting, stopping and restarting them) on behalf of the Panel. Users never interact with Wings directly.

## Glossary

**Panel**: web application that talks to Wings and lets you control your Servers.

**Wings**: service that manages your Servers' containers on behalf of the Panel.

**Node**: machine (computer or server) that runs Wings and connects to the Panel.

**Server**: a Container managed by Wings, shown in the Panel.

**Docker**: platform that runs Servers in isolated containers.

**Docker Image**: file that contains the libraries, dependencies and files needed to run a Container.

**Container**: isolated environment that a Server runs in.

**Egg**: file that configures how a Server is installed and run, using a Docker Image.

**Yolk**: curated collection of Docker Images provided by Pelican for use with Eggs.

## Example Setup

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A(Pelican Panel)
    A --> B1(Basement Server)
    A --> B2(Rented Server)
    B1 --> W1(Wings)
    B2 --> W2(Wings)
    W2  ---> C5(Palworld)
    W2  ---> C6(Discord Bot)
    W1  ---> C7(FTB Minecraft)
    W1  ---> C8(Factorio)
    W1  ---> C9(GTA FiveM)
    W1  ---> C4(Project Zomboid)
```

## Open Source!

The Panel is released under [AGPLv3](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.en.html) and Wings under [MIT](https://opensource.org/license/mit).
Anyone can browse the code, contribute improvements, and help identify bugs and security issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/pelican).

> **Warning: 🔒 Reporting Security Issues 🔒**
>
> If you notice anything that raises a concern, please reach out directly to **team@pelican.dev**
> For security reasons, we ask that you handle security disclosures responsibly and **avoid posting them on GitHub.**

Meet the people behind Pelican on the [Contributors](https://pelican.dev/docs/contributors/) page.

# Getting Started

> What a Pelican server needs and the one-command install: requirements, the virtualization check, installing Docker, starting it on boot and enabling swap.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/getting-started/

Pelican runs on a dedicated Linux server, and the recommended way to install it is with **Docker**.
The quickest way there is the install script below; this page also covers getting Docker ready yourself, if you'd rather [install the Panel](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/) step by step.

> **Danger**
>
> **You should have some basic familiarity with Linux before you proceed!**

> **Tip: Coming from Pterodactyl?**
>
> You don't need a fresh install. Follow [Migrating from Pterodactyl](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/migrating-from-pterodactyl/) to upgrade your existing Panel and keep all your data.

## Requirements

Pelican runs on a wide range of operating systems, so pick whichever you are most comfortable using,
as long as it supports [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/).

Docker may not work under `OpenVZ`, `Virtuozzo` or `LXC` virtualization unless your provider has configured it for nested containers.
`kvm` and bare metal (`none`) work without issues. To check what your server uses, run:

```sh
systemd-detect-virt
```

If that command isn't available, `sudo dmidecode -s system-manufacturer` usually tells you as well.

A domain (or subdomain) for the Panel, such as `panel.example.com` with an `A` record pointing at your server, gives it HTTPS. It's optional to start with: without one the Panel is served on your server's IP address, and you can add the domain later.

## The quick way: one command

On a fresh server, this installs Docker and starts the Panel on your server's IP address. Give it a domain and it sets up HTTPS with Let's Encrypt too:

```sh
# On your server's IP
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo bash

# On your domain, with HTTPS
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- --domain panel.example.com --email you@example.com
```

It asks nothing; add `--interactive` to be asked about each choice (a domain, the simple or the production setup, Wings).

When it's done, open the address it shows (`http://<your server's IP>/installer`, or `https://<your domain>/installer`) to finish. [Installing the Panel](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#the-install-script) explains every option, what the script sets up and how to change it later. Want an AI assistant to walk you through it? See [Installing with an AI Assistant](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/ai-assistant/).

The rest of this page sets up Docker by hand, for the [Docker Compose install](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#docker-compose) or for [Wings](https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/install/). The script does all of it for you.

## Installing Docker

For a quick install of Docker CE, you can use the command below:

```sh
curl -sSL https://get.docker.com/ | CHANNEL=stable sudo sh
```

That works on Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, CentOS Stream and RHEL. On **AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux and Oracle Linux** it stops with "Unable to find a match: docker-ce": Docker's repos for them have no Docker Engine packages. Use Docker's CentOS repo instead, which has the same packages:

```sh
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/docker-ce.repo -o /etc/yum.repos.d/docker-ce.repo
sudo dnf -y install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
```

Some cloud images leave out kernel modules Docker needs:

- On **CentOS Stream, AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux 10**, `xt_addrtype` is missing, so Docker installs but won't start.
- On **Oracle Linux** with its UEK kernel, `xt_ipvs` is missing, so Docker runs but Swarm can't reach its services (the Panel answers 502).

Install them, then restart Docker:

```sh
# CentOS Stream, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux
sudo dnf -y install kernel-modules-extra-$(uname -r)
# Oracle Linux (UEK)
sudo dnf -y install kernel-uek-modules-extra-$(uname -r) kernel-uek-modules-extra-netfilter-$(uname -r)

sudo systemctl restart docker
```

If `sudo modprobe xt_addrtype` (or `xt_ipvs`) still can't find the module, the package was installed for a newer kernel than the one running: reboot and try again. The [install script](#the-quick-way-one-command) does all of this for you.

> **Info: Installing Docker CE**
>
> If none of this works on your server, see the [official Docker documentation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) on how to install Docker CE.

## Start Docker on Boot

If you are on an operating system with systemd (Ubuntu 16+, Debian 8+, CentOS 7+) run the command below to have Docker start when you boot your machine.

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now docker
```

## Enabling Swap

On most systems, Docker will be unable to setup swap space by default. You can confirm this by running `docker info` and looking for the output of `WARNING: No swap limit support` near the bottom.

Enabling swap is entirely optional, but we recommended doing it if you will be hosting for others and to prevent OOM errors.

To enable swap, open `/etc/default/grub` as a root user and find the line starting with `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`. Make
sure the line includes `swapaccount=1` somewhere inside the double-quotes.

After that, run `sudo update-grub` followed by `sudo reboot` to restart the server and have swap enabled.
Below is an example of what the line should look like, _do not copy this line verbatim. It often has additional OS-specific parameters._

```text
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="swapaccount=1"
```

> **Info: GRUB Configurations**
>
> Some Linux distros may ignore `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`.
> Therefore you might have to use `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX` instead should the above variable not work for you.

## Next Steps

Docker is ready. Continue to [Installing the Panel](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/).

Prefer to run the Panel directly on your server without Docker? Follow the [standalone install](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/standalone/getting-started/) instead.

---

# Installing the Panel

> Install the Pelican Panel with Docker: the one-command script (Swarm, Traefik and automatic HTTPS, optionally MariaDB, Redis and Wings), or Compose by hand.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/

Pelican provides pre-built Docker images via GitHub Packages. `ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest` is the current latest release, and `ghcr.io/pelican/panel:main` is built automatically from the current `main` branch. Docker is the recommended way to install the Panel. If you'd rather run it directly on your server, see the [standalone install](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/standalone/getting-started/).

> **Note**
>
> The images used to be published as `ghcr.io/pelican-dev/panel`. That path no longer gets updates, so if your `compose.yml` still uses it, change `image:` to `ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest`.

There are two ways to install it with Docker:

- **[The install script](#the-install-script)** does everything with one command, HTTPS included once you give it a domain, and is the quickest way to a working Panel.
- **[Docker Compose](#docker-compose)** is the same Panel set up by hand, if you want to see and own every step.

## The install script

On a fresh Linux server (see [Getting Started](https://pelican.dev/docs/getting-started/) for the requirements), run:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo bash
```

It asks nothing: with no options it installs the Panel on your server's IP, with the [quick profile](#profiles) and without Wings. To choose, pass [options](#options) (a domain, a profile, Wings), or add `--interactive` to be asked. Then it:

1. checks the server: Linux on x86_64 or arm64, a virtualization Docker works on, ports 80 and 443 free, and the domain pointing at this server if you gave one;
2. installs Docker if it's missing;
3. starts a one-node [Docker Swarm](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/), on address ranges that leave room for Wings' network;
4. deploys a stack named `pelican` from `/opt/pelican`:
    - **Traefik** on ports 80 and 443. Without a domain it serves the Panel on `http://<your server's IP>`. With one, it sends HTTP to HTTPS and gets a Let's Encrypt certificate for the domain on the first visit, then renews it on its own.
    - **The Panel** behind it, in the `ghcr.io/pelican/panel` image.
    - With the production profile, **MariaDB** and **Redis** as well.
5. with Wings, installs it [as in the Wings guide](https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/install/). With a domain, Traefik also serves Wings' own domain, so Wings gets a certificate too.

When it finishes, open the address it shows (`http://<your server's IP>/installer`, or `https://<your domain>/installer`) to create your admin account.

> **Warning: Before you run it**
>
> - Nothing else may use ports 80 or 443 (an earlier NGINX or Apache, or a Panel installed with Docker Compose).
> - Using a domain? Point its `A` record (and Wings' domain's, if you install Wings) at the server, and wait until it resolves.
> - With Cloudflare, keep the record **DNS only** (grey cloud) so Let's Encrypt can reach the server. You can turn the proxy on once the certificate is there.

### Without a domain

Run the script without `--domain` and the Panel is served on `http://<your server's IP>`, the external IPv4 address the script finds (pass `--ip` to choose another, such as a server behind NAT). It's the quickest way to try Pelican, but it's plain HTTP: logins and data cross the network unencrypted. Add a domain before you rely on it.

To add one later, point its `A` record at the server and run the script again with the domain. It keeps your keys, passwords and data, switches the Panel to HTTPS and sends visitors of the old address to the new one:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- --domain panel.example.com --email you@example.com
```

Or set `PANEL_DOMAIN` and `LE_EMAIL` in `/opt/pelican/pelican.env` and run `sudo /opt/pelican/deploy.sh`.

### Profiles

| Profile | What it runs | For |
|:--------|:-------------|:----|
| `quick` | Traefik and the Panel, with SQLite, file sessions and a database queue | One server and a small community; the least to run and back up |
| `production` | Traefik, the Panel, MariaDB 11.4 and Redis 7 (cache, sessions and queue) | More users, servers and nodes; the database and passwords are set up for you |

You can't switch an install from one profile to the other by running the script again: the other profile starts with an empty database.

### Options

The script never asks unless you pass `--interactive`: anything you don't give takes its default. Give your choices as options after `bash -s --`, or as environment variables, which suits cloud-init and other provisioning tools. That's also how to hand it to an [AI assistant](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/ai-assistant/):

```sh
# On the server's IP, with the defaults (the quick profile, no Wings)
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo bash

# With a domain and HTTPS, MariaDB and Redis
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- \
  --domain panel.example.com --email you@example.com --profile production

# The same with environment variables (with sudo, put them after it)
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo PELICAN_DOMAIN=panel.example.com \
  PELICAN_EMAIL=you@example.com PELICAN_PROFILE=production bash

# Asked one question at a time, with explanations
curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- --interactive
```

| Option | Variable | What it does |
|:-------|:---------|:-------------|
| `--domain DOMAIN` | `PELICAN_DOMAIN` | Serve the Panel at this domain with HTTPS, e.g. `panel.example.com`. Without it, the Panel is on `http://<server IP>` |
| `--email EMAIL` | `PELICAN_EMAIL` | Your email, for Let's Encrypt's certificate notices (needed with a domain) |
| `--ip IP` | `PELICAN_IP` | The address the Panel is served on without a domain (default: the server's external IPv4 address) |
| `--profile quick\|production` | `PELICAN_PROFILE` | Which [profile](#profiles) to run (default `quick`) |
| `--wings`, `--no-wings` | `PELICAN_WINGS=1` or `0` | Also install Wings on this server (default: no). Without a domain it's on `http://<server IP>:8080` |
| `--wings-domain DOMAIN` | `PELICAN_WINGS_DOMAIN` | Wings' own domain, such as `node.example.com`: needed for Wings when the Panel has a domain |
| `--dir PATH` | `PELICAN_DIR` | Where the stack's files go (default `/opt/pelican`) |
| `--image IMAGE` | `PELICAN_IMAGE` | Another Panel image, e.g. a fixed version |
| `--staging` | `PELICAN_STAGING=1` | Use Let's Encrypt's staging server: test certificates, without its rate limits |
| `--skip-dns-check` | `PELICAN_SKIP_DNS_CHECK=1` | Don't check the domains point here (behind NAT, or DNS set up afterwards). Without it, a domain that doesn't point here stops the install |
| `--dry-run` | `PELICAN_DRY_RUN=1` | Show what it would do and write the files to a temp folder, changing nothing. Needs no root, so you can try it anywhere |
| `--interactive` | `PELICAN_INTERACTIVE=1` | Ask for each choice instead, with explanations |

When both are set, the option wins. `PELICAN_TRAEFIK_IMAGE` runs another Traefik than the exact version the script pins.

To read the script before running it, download it first:

```sh
curl -fsSL -o install.sh https://pelican.dev/install.sh
less install.sh
bash install.sh --dry-run --domain panel.example.com --email you@example.com
sudo bash install.sh --domain panel.example.com --email you@example.com
```

### Your files

Everything the script sets up is in `/opt/pelican`:

| File | What it is |
|:-----|:-----------|
| `pelican.env` | Your settings, the `APP_KEY` and the database passwords. Readable by root only. |
| `stack.yml` | The services, with every value taken from `pelican.env` |
| `deploy.sh` | Applies `pelican.env` and `stack.yml` to the running stack |
| `traefik/pelican.yml` | Traefik's routes, written by `deploy.sh` from `pelican.env` (add your own files next to it) |

> **Danger: Back up pelican.env**
>
> `APP_KEY` encrypts parts of your Panel's data. Copy `pelican.env` somewhere safe, off the server: if it's lost, that data can't be recovered, **even with database backups**.

### Changing settings later

Change a value in `pelican.env` and apply it:

```sh
sudo nano /opt/pelican/pelican.env
sudo /opt/pelican/deploy.sh
```

For example, a new `PANEL_DOMAIN` (with `LE_EMAIL`) switches the Panel to HTTPS and gets its certificate as soon as its DNS points at the server, and `PANEL_IMAGE=ghcr.io/pelican/panel:<version>` keeps the Panel on one version. Running the install script again also works: it keeps your keys and passwords, updates the stack and moves Traefik to the version it pins.

### Updating

`deploy.sh` checks the registry for each image, so running it again pulls a newer Panel when there is one:

```sh
sudo /opt/pelican/deploy.sh
```

Database migrations run when the new Panel starts. See [Updating the Panel](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/update/) for the versions each release needs.

### Wings on the same server

With `--wings`, the script installs Wings and enables its service. Wings itself starts once it has a configuration from the Panel.

Without a domain, Wings is reached directly on `http://<server IP>:8080`. In the Panel, create the node with the server's IP as the FQDN, **HTTP**, **Not Behind Proxy** and port `8080`; then copy its configuration to `/etc/pelican/config.yml` and start Wings. When you add a domain for the Panel later, Wings needs one too (HTTPS on the Panel means HTTPS on Wings): run the script again with `--wings-domain` and update the node.

With a domain, Traefik serves Wings' domain over HTTPS:

1. In the Panel, go to **Admin → Nodes → Create**. Use Wings' domain as the FQDN, choose **HTTPS** and **Behind Proxy**, and set the port the Panel connects to as `443` and the port Wings listens on as `8080`.
2. Copy the node's configuration to `/etc/pelican/config.yml`, or run its **Auto Deploy** command. Traefik handles HTTPS, so in that file `api.port` is `8080` and `api.ssl.enabled` is `false`.
3. Start Wings: `sudo systemctl start wings`.
4. Open SFTP (port `2022`) and the ports you allocate to game servers in your provider's firewall. When `ufw` is active the script opens 80, 443 and 2022 in it; game server ports are yours to open.

Wings on other servers is installed [the usual way](https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/install/).

### When something doesn't work

```sh
docker service ls                          # each service should show 1/1
docker service ps pelican_panel --no-trunc # why a service doesn't start
docker service logs -f pelican_panel       # the Panel's logs
docker service logs pelican_traefik 2>&1 | grep -i acme   # certificate problems
```

No certificate? Check that the domain points at the server, ports 80 and 443 are reachable from the internet and the record isn't proxied by a CDN. Let's Encrypt limits how often it issues certificates for one domain: test with `--staging`, then run the script again without it, which moves the install to real certificates (the test ones are kept apart and not used again).

Docker's address ranges can clash with a network your server is already on. The script uses `10.203.0.0/16` for Swarm and `10.204.0.0/24` for `docker_gwbridge`; set `PELICAN_SWARM_POOL`, `PELICAN_GWBRIDGE_SUBNET` and `PELICAN_PUBLIC_SUBNET` before running it to use others.

### Backups and removing it

The Panel's data lives in Docker volumes: `pelican_pelican-data` (the Panel's `.env`, SQLite database and uploads), `pelican_pelican-plugins`, and with the production profile `pelican_pelican-db` (MariaDB). Back them up together with `pelican.env`. For example, for the Panel's data:

```sh
docker run --rm -v pelican_pelican-data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pelican-data.tar.gz -C /data .
```

To remove the stack, keeping its data: `docker stack rm pelican`. Removing the volumes as well (`docker volume rm pelican_pelican-data ...`) **deletes the Panel and all of its data**.

## Docker Compose

This guide requires Docker CE. (Docker Compose has been included in the Docker CLI since v2. Docker Compose v1 is unsupported.) For instructions on installing and configuring Docker, see [Getting Started](https://pelican.dev/docs/getting-started/).

### Basics

The easiest deployment method is using the standard `compose.yml` file.

This configuration includes an integrated web server that will automatically obtain SSL certificates if you are serving over HTTPS. For the database, it assumes you want to use SQLite (or you have an external database server to configure using the  installer.) It also assumes you intend to use the Filesystem driver for cache, filesystem or database driver for session, and database driver for queue (or you have an external Redis server to configure using the installer.) If you want to use other options built into Docker, see [Advanced Options](#advanced-options).

### Create compose.yml

```yml title="compose.yml"
services:
  panel:
    image: ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest
    restart: always
    networks:
      - default
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    volumes:
      - pelican-data:/pelican-data
      - pelican-logs:/var/www/html/storage/logs
      - pelican-plugins:/var/www/html/plugins
    environment:
      XDG_DATA_HOME: /pelican-data
      APP_URL: "http://localhost"
      ADMIN_EMAIL: "USEYOUROWNEMAILHERE@example.com"

volumes:
  pelican-data:
  pelican-logs:
  pelican-plugins:

networks:
  default:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.20.0.0/16
```

### Set Required Environment Variables

1. Set `APP_URL` to the base URL your panel will be reachable on, including the protocol (https:// or http://) and port.
    - Note that Caddy, the integrated webserver, will serve a 308 redirect to any requests on port 80 if the `APP_URL` begins with `https://`. If your final site will be reachable over HTTPS but TLS (SSL) will be handled and terminated by an upstream server, such as a reverse proxy, see [Reverse Proxy Configuration](#reverse-proxy-configuration).
2. Set the `ADMIN_EMAIL` to your email address. Caddy will use this email address to generate a LetsEncrypt SSL certificate if you are serving via HTTPS.

Now, close and save changes to `compose.yml`.

### Starting

From the directory in which the compose file is located, run:

```sh
docker compose up -d
```

### Back Up Your Encryption Key

The first time the container starts, it will generate an `APP_KEY` which is used as an encryption key. This will be saved automatically, but you should save a copy in a secure place in case you need it later.

```sh
docker compose logs panel | grep 'Generated app key:'
```

### Installing

Open the installer in your browser at `APP_URL/installer` to finish setting up the panel.

> **Note**
>
> The first time the container starts after installing or updating, it will apply database migrations, which may take a few minutes. The panel will not be accessible during this process.

#### Sensible Driver Defaults:

* Cache Driver: Filesystem
* Database Driver: SQLite
* Queue Driver: Database
* Session Driver: Filesystem

For other configuration, such as UI options, CAPTCHA, email, backups and OAuth, head to the settings menu in the admin panel.

### Stopping

The panel will automatically restart if the container crashes or the host restarts.  If you need to non-destructively stop the panel for any reason, navigate back to the directory containing `compose.yml` and run:

```sh
docker compose down
```

### Uninstalling

To uninstall the panel, navigate to the directory containing `compose.yml` and run:

```sh
docker compose down -v
```

> **Danger**
>
> **This will permanently delete the panel and all associated data including the SQLite database and your encryption key.**

## Advanced Options

### Custom Caddyfile

The default Caddyfile will work for standard installations. If you need to edit the configuration of the integrated webserver, such as to place it behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS, you can do so by bind-mounting a Caddyfile on the host to `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile` inside the container.

This example assumes there is a Caddyfile in the same directory as the `compose.yml` file.

```yml title="compose.yml"
services:
  panel:
    image: ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest
    restart: always
    networks:
      - default
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    volumes:
      - pelican-data:/pelican-data
      - pelican-logs:/var/www/html/storage/logs
      - pelican-plugins:/var/www/html/plugins
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
    environment:
      XDG_DATA_HOME: /pelican-data
      APP_URL: "http://localhost"
      ADMIN_EMAIL: "USEYOUROWNEMAILHERE@example.com"

volumes:
  pelican-data:
  pelican-logs:
  pelican-plugins:

networks:
  default:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.20.0.0/16
```

An example Caddyfile for hosting the panel behind a reverse proxy is shown below. It exposes the panel on port 80 regardless of the Host header, and will not attempt to obtain a TLS certificate. `[UPSTREAM IP]` must be replaced with the IP address of the reverse proxy.

```caddyfile title="Caddyfile"
{
    admin off
    servers {
        trusted_proxies static [UPSTREAM IP]
    }
}

:80 {
    root * /var/www/html/public
    encode gzip

    php_fastcgi 127.0.0.1:9000
    file_server
}
```

> **Info**
>
> **Note:** If the trusted directive is not set or improperly configured, file uploads will fail. Commonly, when the reverse proxy is running outside of Docker, the IP address will not match `127.0.0.1`, but will instead match a Docker bridge interface or `docker0`.

#### Raising file upload limits

The default file upload limit is 2MB. To raise this limit, modify the `Caddyfile` file as such:

```caddyfile title="Caddyfile"
<domain> {
    ...

    encode gzip

    php_fastcgi 127.0.0.1:9000 {
        env PHP_VALUE "upload_max_filesize = 256M
                       post_max_size = 256M"
    }
    file_server
}
```

### Reverse Proxy Configuration

When running the panel behind a reverse proxy that handles TLS (SSL), set the following environment variables:

1. Set `APP_URL` to the URL users will visit, e.g. `https://panel.example.com`.
2. Set `BEHIND_PROXY` to `"true"`. This does 2 things:
    1. The panel listens on port `80` inside the container, regardless of the `APP_URL`. Map whichever host port your proxy forwards to onto container port `80`.
    2. The panel will not attempt to obtain a certificate from Let's Encrypt. Without this, an `https://` `APP_URL` requires the `LE_EMAIL` environment variable and the panel will exit if it is missing.
3. Set `TRUSTED_PROXIES` to a comma-separated list of the IP addresses (or CIDR ranges) of your reverse proxy, so the panel trusts its forwarded headers.

No custom Caddyfile is needed for this setup. An example `compose.yml` for hosting the panel behind a reverse proxy is shown below.

```yml title="compose.yml"
services:
  panel:
    image: ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest
    restart: always
    networks:
      - default
    ports:
      - "81:80" # Change 81 to the host port your reverse proxy forwards to
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    volumes:
      - pelican-data:/pelican-data
      - pelican-logs:/var/www/html/storage/logs
      - pelican-plugins:/var/www/html/plugins
    environment:
      XDG_DATA_HOME: /pelican-data
      APP_URL: "https://panel.example.com"
      BEHIND_PROXY: "true"
      TRUSTED_PROXIES: "127.0.0.1,172.17.0.1,172.20.0.1" # Change to the IP(s) of your proxy. These defaults cover a proxy on the same host
      ADMIN_EMAIL: "USEYOUROWNEMAILHERE@example.com"

volumes:
  pelican-data:
  pelican-logs:
  pelican-plugins:

networks:
  default:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.20.0.0/16
```

> **Info**
>
> **Note:** If `TRUSTED_PROXIES` is not set or does not match your proxy, file uploads will fail. When the reverse proxy runs outside of Docker, its requests usually come from a Docker bridge interface (such as `docker0`, commonly `172.17.0.1`) rather than `127.0.0.1`.

---

# Standalone Install

> Install the Pelican Panel without Docker: supported operating systems, PHP and webserver dependencies, downloading the panel files and installing Composer.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/standalone/getting-started/

Pelican Panel is designed to run on your webserver.

You are expected to read through our documentation.
We have spent a lot of time curating these docs for the community,
so please take some time to read through them before asking for help on the forums!

> **Danger**
>
> **You should have some basic familiarity with Linux before you proceed!**

> **Tip: Coming from Pterodactyl?**
>
> You don't need a fresh install. Follow [Migrating from Pterodactyl](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/migrating-from-pterodactyl/) to upgrade your existing Panel and keep all your data.

> **Info: Installing with an AI assistant?**
>
> Give it these docs and a tested prompt for a production install: see [Installing with an AI Assistant](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/ai-assistant/). The **Copy page** button above copies any page for it.

This guide installs Pelican directly on your server. The recommended method is [Docker](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/), with a one-command install script; use this guide if you'd rather not run the Panel in a container.

## Picking an Operating System (OS)

Pelican runs on a wide range of operating systems, so pick whichever you are most comfortable using. Note: Other OS's, not listed below, might still work.

This documentation assumes a Debian/Ubuntu based OS with apt as package manager.

> **Warning**
>
> OpenVZ, **unless specifically configured**, will **not** work with Pelican.

| Operating System | Version | Supported | Notes                                                               |
|:----------------:|:-------:|:---------:|:--------------------------------------------------------------------:|
| **Ubuntu**       | 22.04   |     ✅︎︎    |                                                                      |
|                  | 24.04   |     ✅︎    |                                                                      |
|                  | 26.04   |     ✅︎    |                                                                      |
| **Debian**       | 11      |     ⚠️   | **No SQLite Support**                                                |
|                  | 12      |     ✅︎    |                                                                      |
|                  | 13      |     ✅︎    |                                                                      |
| **Alma Linux**   | 8       |     ⚠️   | **No SQLite Support**                                                |
|                  | 9       |     ⚠️   | **No SQLite Support**                                                |
|                  | 10      |     ✅︎    |                                                                      |
| **Rocky Linux**  | 8       |     ⚠️   | **No SQLite Support**                                                |
|                  | 9       |     ⚠️   | **No SQLite Support**                                                |
|                  | 10      |     ✅︎    |                                                                      |
| **CentOS**       | 10      |     ✅︎    |                                                                      |

SQLite support depends on [libsqlite3-0_3.35+](https://pkgs.org/download/libsqlite3-0) being on the host system.
"No SQLite Support" means you'll have to build the package from source.

## Dependencies

For the Panel you need to install **PHP `8.5` (recommended) or `8.4`**, with the following **extensions**:
`gd`, `mysql`, `mbstring`, `bcmath`, `xml`, `curl`, `zip`, `intl`, `sqlite3` and `fpm`.

You will also need a Webserver. Currently, **Apache, NGINX or Caddy** are supported.

If you want to use MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL for the panel database make sure to install either **MySQL 8.4+, MariaDB 10.11+ or PostgreSQL 17+**. (both client and server!)

Finally, for some commands during the installation you need `curl`, `tar` and `unzip`.

> **Warning**
>
> Please make sure you installed **all** needed dependencies before continuing!

## Create Directories & Downloading Files

The first step in this process is to create the folder where the panel will live and then move ourselves into that
newly created folder.

```sh
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/pelican
cd /var/www/pelican
```

Once you have created a new directory to use and moved into it, you'll need to download the Panel files.
This is as simple as using `curl` to download the latest release.

```sh
curl -L https://github.com/pelican/panel/releases/latest/download/panel.tar.gz | sudo tar -xzv
```

## Install Composer

Next we will set up Composer along with the required dependencies.

``` bash
curl -sS https://getcomposer.org/installer | sudo php -- --install-dir=/usr/local/bin --filename=composer
```

```sh
sudo COMPOSER_ALLOW_SUPERUSER=1 composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
```

> **Info**
>
> Even though composer might tell you that you have outdated dependencies, do **not** run `composer update`!

---

# Webserver Configuration

> Set up NGINX, Apache or Caddy for the Pelican Panel installed without Docker, with or without SSL, from config files filled in with your domain and PHP version.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/standalone/webserver-config/

Fill in your setup below. The config files on this page update to match, so you can copy them as they are.
Underlined values come from your setup.

> **Info**
>
> When using the SSL (https) configuration you MUST create SSL certificates, otherwise your webserver will fail to start.
> See the [Creating SSL Certificates](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/ssl/) documentation page to learn how to create these certificates before continuing.

## NGINX

> **Info: PHP version**
>
> Pick your PHP version in **Your setup** above and the PHP-FPM socket line (highlighted below) uses it.

First, remove the default NGINX configuration.
```sh
sudo rm /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default
```
Now, you should paste the contents of the file below, with your domain filled in from **Your setup** (or replace `<domain>` yourself), into a file called
`pelican.conf` and place the file in `/etc/nginx/sites-available/`.

### HTTPS

> **Warning**
>
> **Note:** IPs cannot be used with SSL.

```nginx title="/etc/nginx/sites-available/pelican.conf"
server_tokens off;

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name <domain>;
    return 301 https://$server_name$request_uri;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name <domain>;

    root /var/www/pelican/public;
    index index.php;

    access_log /var/log/nginx/pelican.app-access.log;
    error_log  /var/log/nginx/pelican.app-error.log error;

    # allow larger file uploads and longer script runtimes
    client_max_body_size 100m;
    client_body_timeout 120s;

    sendfile off;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/<domain>/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/<domain>/privkey.pem;
    ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m;
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
    ssl_ciphers "ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:DHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:DHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384";
    ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on;

    # See https://hstspreload.org/ before uncommenting the line below.
    # add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=15768000; preload;";
    add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
    add_header X-XSS-Protection "1; mode=block";
    add_header X-Robots-Tag none;
    add_header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self'";
    add_header X-Frame-Options DENY;
    add_header Referrer-Policy same-origin;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string;
    }

    location ~ \.php$ {
        fastcgi_split_path_info ^(.+\.php)(/.+)$;
        fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php8.5-fpm.sock;
        fastcgi_index index.php;
        include fastcgi_params;
        fastcgi_param PHP_VALUE "upload_max_filesize = 100M \n post_max_size=100M";
        fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name;
        fastcgi_param HTTP_PROXY "";
        fastcgi_intercept_errors off;
        fastcgi_buffer_size 16k;
        fastcgi_buffers 4 16k;
        fastcgi_connect_timeout 300;
        fastcgi_send_timeout 300;
        fastcgi_read_timeout 300;
        include /etc/nginx/fastcgi_params;
    }

    location ~ /\.ht {
        deny all;
    }
}
```

### HTTP

```nginx title="/etc/nginx/sites-available/pelican.conf"
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name <domain>;

    root /var/www/pelican/public;
    index index.html index.htm index.php;
    charset utf-8;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string;
    }

    location = /favicon.ico { access_log off; log_not_found off; }
    location = /robots.txt  { access_log off; log_not_found off; }

    access_log off;
    error_log  /var/log/nginx/pelican.app-error.log error;

    # allow larger file uploads and longer script runtimes
    client_max_body_size 100m;
    client_body_timeout 120s;

    sendfile off;

    location ~ \.php$ {
        fastcgi_split_path_info ^(.+\.php)(/.+)$;
        fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php8.5-fpm.sock;
        fastcgi_index index.php;
        include fastcgi_params;
        fastcgi_param PHP_VALUE "upload_max_filesize = 100M \n post_max_size=100M";
        fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name;
        fastcgi_param HTTP_PROXY "";
        fastcgi_intercept_errors off;
        fastcgi_buffer_size 16k;
        fastcgi_buffers 4 16k;
        fastcgi_connect_timeout 300;
        fastcgi_send_timeout 300;
        fastcgi_read_timeout 300;
    }

    location ~ /\.ht {
        deny all;
    }
}
```

### Enabling Configuration

The final step is to enable your NGINX configuration and restart it.

```sh
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/pelican.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/pelican.conf
```

#### You need to restart nginx to load the new config file.

```sh
sudo systemctl restart nginx
```

## Apache

First, remove the default Apache configuration.

```sh
a2dissite 000-default default-ssl 000-default-le-ssl
```

Now, you should paste the contents of the file below, with your domain filled in from **Your setup** (or replace `<domain>` yourself), into a file called
`pelican.conf` and place the file in `/etc/apache2/sites-available/`.

Note: When using Apache, make sure you have the `libapache2-mod-php` package installed or else PHP will not display on your webserver.

### HTTPS

> **Warning**
>
> **Note:** IPs cannot be used with SSL.

```apacheconf title="/etc/apache2/sites-available/pelican.conf"
    <VirtualHost *:80>
        ServerName <domain>

        RewriteEngine On
        RewriteCond %{HTTPS} !=on
        RewriteRule ^/?(.*) https://%{SERVER_NAME}/$1 [R,L]
        </VirtualHost>

        <VirtualHost *:443>
        ServerName <domain>
        DocumentRoot "/var/www/pelican/public"

        AllowEncodedSlashes On

        php_value upload_max_filesize 100M
        php_value post_max_size 100M

        <Directory "/var/www/pelican/public">
            Require all granted
            AllowOverride all
        </Directory>

        SSLEngine on
        SSLCertificateFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/<domain>/fullchain.pem
        SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/<domain>/privkey.pem
    </VirtualHost>
```

### HTTP

```apacheconf title="/etc/apache2/sites-available/pelican.conf"
    <VirtualHost *:80>
        ServerName <domain>
        DocumentRoot "/var/www/pelican/public"

        AllowEncodedSlashes On

        php_value upload_max_filesize 100M
        php_value post_max_size 100M

        <Directory "/var/www/pelican/public">
            AllowOverride all
            Require all granted
        </Directory>
    </VirtualHost>
```

### Enabling Configuration

Once you've created the file above, simply run the commands below.

> **Info: PHP version**
>
> Pick your PHP version in **Your setup** above and the highlighted `a2enmod` line uses it.

```sh
sudo a2ensite pelican.conf
sudo a2enmod rewrite
sudo a2enmod php8.5
```

#### You need to restart apache to load the new config file.

```sh
sudo systemctl restart apache2
```

## Caddy

> **Info: PHP version**
>
> Pick your PHP version in **Your setup** above and the PHP-FPM socket line (highlighted below) uses it.

First, remove the default Caddy configuration.

```sh
sudo rm /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
```

The config file path is `/etc/caddy/`.

### HTTPS

> **Warning**
>
> **Note:** IPs cannot be used with SSL.

```caddy title="/etc/caddy/Caddyfile"
{
    servers :443 {
        timeouts {
            read_body 120s
        }
    }
}

<domain> {
    root * /var/www/pelican/public

    file_server

    php_fastcgi unix//run/php/php8.5-fpm.sock {
        root /var/www/pelican/public
        index index.php

        env PHP_VALUE "upload_max_filesize = 100M
        post_max_size = 100M"
        env HTTP_PROXY ""
        env HTTPS "on"

        read_timeout 300s
        dial_timeout 300s
        write_timeout 300s
    }

    header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=16768000; preload;"
    header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
    header X-XSS-Protection "1; mode=block;"
    header X-Robots-Tag "none"
    header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self'"
    header X-Frame-Options "DENY"
    header Referrer-Policy "same-origin"

    request_body {
        max_size 100m
    }

    respond /.ht* 403

    log {
        output file /var/log/caddy/pelican.log {
            roll_size 100MiB
            roll_keep_for 7d
        }
        level INFO
    }
}
```

### HTTP

```caddy title="/etc/caddy/Caddyfile"
{
    servers :80 {
        timeouts {
            read_body 120s
        }
    }
}

<domain>:80 {
    root * /var/www/pelican/public

    file_server

    php_fastcgi unix//run/php/php8.5-fpm.sock {
        root /var/www/pelican/public
        index index.php

        env PHP_VALUE "upload_max_filesize = 100M
        post_max_size = 100M"
        env HTTP_PROXY ""

        read_timeout 300s
        dial_timeout 300s
        write_timeout 300s
    }

    header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=16768000; preload;"
    header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
    header X-XSS-Protection "1; mode=block;"
    header X-Robots-Tag "none"
    header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self'"
    header X-Frame-Options "DENY"
    header Referrer-Policy "same-origin"

    request_body {
        max_size 100m
    }

    respond /.ht* 403

    log {
        output file /var/log/caddy/pelican.log {
            roll_size 100MiB
            roll_keep_for 7d
        }
        level INFO
    }
}
```

### Enabling Configuration
The final step is to restart Caddy.

```sh
sudo systemctl restart caddy
```

# Panel Setup

> Generate the Panel .env file and APP_KEY with p:environment:setup, set file permissions and finish the install in the web installer.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/standalone/panel-setup/

The core environment is easily configured using a single CLI command & the web installer built into the app.
These steps will cover setting up things such as sessions, caching, database credentials, and email sending.

Running `php artisan p:environment:setup` will, if it does not exist, auto create the required `.env` file and generate a `APP_KEY`.

```sh
sudo php artisan p:environment:setup
```

> **Warning: BACK UP APP_KEY!**
>
> **Back up** your encryption key (APP_KEY in the `.env` file). This is used as an encryption key for all data that needs to be stored securely (e.g. api keys).
> Store it somewhere safe - not just on your server. If you lose it all encrypted data is irrecoverable -- **even if you have database backups.**

## Setting Permissions

The next step in the installation process is to set the correct permissions on the Panel files so that the webserver can
use them correctly.

```sh
sudo chmod -R 755 storage/* bootstrap/cache/
```

### NGINX/Apache/Caddy

```sh
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/pelican
```

### Rocky Linux NGINX

```sh
sudo chown -R nginx:nginx /var/www/pelican
```

### Rocky Linux Apache

```sh
sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www/pelican
```

## Web-Installer

Once you've set the proper permissions, continue the Panel install on the web interface.
The web installer is located at `<domain>/installer` or `<ip>/installer`.

> **Info: Want something advanced?**
>
> Make sure to read the [MySQL guide](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/mysql/) first if you want to use MySQL/ MariaDB instead of SQLite!
> If you want to use Redis make sure to read the [Redis guide](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/redis/) first.

# Optional Panel Configuration

> Configure optional Pelican Panel settings: local or S3 backups, reverse proxy setup for NGINX and Cloudflare, captcha and two-factor requirements.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/standalone/optional-config/

The Panel works without any of these settings. This page covers the ones you may want later: where backups are stored (on the node or in S3), running the Panel behind a reverse proxy, captcha, two-factor requirements and health monitoring.

## Backups

Pelican allows users to create backups of their servers. To create backups, a backup storage method has to be configured.

When changing Pelican's backup storage method, users may still download or delete existing backups from the prior storage driver. In the instance of migrating from S3 to local backups, S3 credentials must remain configured after switching to the local backup storage method.

Make sure to clear the config cache (`cd /var/www/pelican && php artisan config:clear`) and to restart the queue worker (`systemctl restart pelican-queue`) after changing the backup driver to apply the changes.

### Using Local Backups

By default, Pelican uses local storage via Wings for backups. That said, this method of backup storage can be explicitly set within the Settings Page on the Admin side of the panel.

Please note that, when using local storage via Wings, the destination for backups is set in the Wings config file with the following setting key:

```yml
system:
  backup_directory: /path/to/backup/storage
```

### Using S3 Backups

AWS S3 (or compatible storage) can be used to store remote or cloud-based backups. This can be configured in the Settings Page on the Admin side of the panel.

For some configurations, you might have to change your S3 URL from `bucket.domain.com` to `domain.com/bucket`. To accomplish this, add `AWS_USE_PATH_STYLE_ENDPOINT=true` to your `.env` file.

#### Multipart Upload

The S3 backup is using the S3 multipart upload capabilities. In rare situations, you might want to adjust the size of a single part or the lifespan of the generated pre-signed URLs. The default part size is 5GB, and the default pre-signed URL lifespan is 60 minutes.

You can configure the maximal part size using the `BACKUP_MAX_PART_SIZE` environment variable. You must specify the size in bytes. To define the pre-signed URL lifespan, use the `BACKUP_PRESIGNED_URL_LIFESPAN` variable. The expected unit is minutes.

The following `.env` snippet configures 1GB parts and uses 120 minutes as the pre-signed URL lifespan:

```sh
BACKUP_MAX_PART_SIZE=1073741824
BACKUP_PRESIGNED_URL_LIFESPAN=120
```

#### Storage Class

Should you need to specify a storage class, use the `AWS_BACKUPS_STORAGE_CLASS` environment variable. The default option is `STANDARD` (S3 Standard).

```sh
AWS_BACKUPS_STORAGE_CLASS=
```

## Reverse Proxy Setup

When running Pelican behind a reverse proxy, such as [Cloudflare's Flexible SSL](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/origin-configuration/ssl-modes/)
or NGINX/Apache/Caddy, etc., you will need to make a quick modification to the Panel to ensure things continue to work as expected. By default, when using these reverse proxies,
your Panel will not correctly handle requests. You'll most likely be unable to login or see security warnings in your browser console as it attempts to load insecure assets.
This is because the internal logic the Panel uses to determine how links should be generated thinks it is running over HTTP and not over HTTPS.

You will need to edit trusted proxies, on the Settings page. We highly suggest providing a specific IP address
(or comma-separated list of IPs) rather than allowing `*`. For example, if your proxy is running on the same machine as the server,
the chances are that using `127.0.0.1` would work for you.

### NGINX Specific Configuration

To properly respond to an NGINX reverse proxy, the NGINX `location` config must contain the following lines:

```NGINX
proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
proxy_set_header Host $host;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
proxy_redirect off;
proxy_buffering off;
proxy_request_buffering off;
```

### Cloudflare Specific Configuration

If you're using Cloudflare's Flexible SSL you should set `TRUSTED_PROXIES` to contain [their IP addresses](https://www.cloudflare.com/ips/).

You can easily do this on the Settings page in the Panel.

## Captcha

The Panel has options to enable captcha to secure the login page from brute-force attacks. By default only Cloudflare Turnstile is available.

### Disable Captcha

If you cannot access your panel, you have to modify the `.env` directly to disable it.

Edit the `.env` in the panel's root directory `/var/www/pelican/` and change the value of `CAPTCHA_TURNSTILE_ENABLED` to `false`.

After that run `php artisan config:clear` to refresh the config cache.

## 2FA

If possible you should use the panel to update your 2FA settings. If you can't access your panel for whatever reason you can use the following steps.

### Disable 2FA requirement

Edit the `.env` in the panel's root directory `/var/www/pelican/` and change the value of `APP_2FA_REQUIRED` to `0`.

### Disable 2FA for a specific user

Run the following command in your `/var/www/pelican` directory.

```sh
php artisan p:user:disable2fa
```

## Health Monitoring

The Panel checks its database, cache, queue, schedule, disk space and versions every five minutes. Admins can see the results on the **Health** page in the admin area.

### Health Endpoint

To let an external monitor (Uptime Kuma, UptimeRobot, etc.) read these results, set a secret in the `.env` in `/var/www/pelican/` and run `php artisan config:clear`:

```sh
HEALTH_ENDPOINT_SECRET=a-long-random-string
```

The results are then available as JSON at `https://panel.example.com/health`. Send the secret as a bearer token:

```sh
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer a-long-random-string" https://panel.example.com/health
```

If your monitor can't send headers, use `https://panel.example.com/health?token=a-long-random-string` instead. Query strings can end up in access logs, so prefer the header.

- `200`: every check is ok or only has a warning (for example, an update is available)
- `503`: at least one check failed, or the checks haven't run in the last 10 minutes (usually a stopped scheduler)
- `403`: wrong or missing secret
- `404`: `HEALTH_ENDPOINT_SECRET` isn't set

The endpoint serves the results from the last scheduled run. Add `fresh` (`/health?fresh`) to run the checks first, which takes longer since it contacts every node.

In Uptime Kuma, an **HTTP(s)** monitor pointed at the endpoint with the `Authorization` header set is enough, since a failing check returns `503`.

---

# Updating the Panel

> Update the Pelican Panel with Docker, the update script or manual steps, and check which Wings and PHP versions each release needs.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/update/

This documentation covers the process for updating the panel portion of Pelican.

> **Tip: Coming from Pterodactyl?**
>
> Updating from Pterodactyl works differently, follow [Migrating from Pterodactyl](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/migrating-from-pterodactyl/) instead.

Before updating, check the release notes on [GitHub](https://github.com/pelican/panel/releases). See [Versioning & Releases](https://pelican.dev/docs/versioning/) for what can change between versions.

## Version Requirements

Each version of Pelican Panel also has a corresponding minimum version of Wings that is required for it to run.

Please see the chart below for how these versions line up.

| Panel Version | Wings Version | Supported | PHP Version     |
|:-------------:|:-------------:|:---------:|:---------------:|
|      1.x      |      1.x      |    ✅︎     |     8.5/8.4     |

## Updating

There are three ways to update, one per tab below: the Docker image (if you installed with Docker), the update script (recommended without Docker) or the manual steps.

### Docker

Installed with the [install script](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#the-install-script)? Run `sudo /opt/pelican/deploy.sh`: it pulls the new image and restarts the Panel.

A [Docker Compose install](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#docker-compose) updates by pulling the new image. From the directory containing your `compose.yml`, run:

```sh
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
```

Database migrations run automatically when the new container starts.

### Update script (recommended)

Simply run the command below and the update script will guide you through the process:

```sh
sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/update-panel.sh)"
```

The script checks your PHP version, extensions, and disk space and verifies the download before it touches the panel.
Your `.env`, storage, plugins, and database are kept, and a backup is saved to a `backup_<timestamp>` folder inside the panel directory.

To run it without prompts, for example from automation, pass `--yes` (and `--dir` if the panel is not in `/var/www/pelican`):

```sh
sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://pelican.dev/update-panel.sh)" update-panel --yes --dir /var/www/pelican
```

### Manual update

### Enter Maintenance Mode

Whenever you are performing an update you should be sure to place your Panel into maintenance mode. This will prevent
users from encountering unexpected errors.

```sh
cd /var/www/pelican
sudo php artisan down
```

### Download Update

The first step in the update process is to download the new panel files from GitHub. The command below will download
the release archive for the most recent version of Pelican, save it in the current directory and will automatically
unpack the archive into your current folder.

```sh
curl -L https://github.com/pelican/panel/releases/latest/download/panel.tar.gz | sudo tar -xzv
```

To verify the archive before extracting it, download it together with its `checksum.txt` release asset instead:

```sh
sudo curl -fLO https://github.com/pelican/panel/releases/latest/download/panel.tar.gz
sudo curl -fLO https://github.com/pelican/panel/releases/latest/download/checksum.txt
sudo sha256sum -c checksum.txt && sudo tar -xzvf panel.tar.gz && sudo rm panel.tar.gz checksum.txt
```

Once the archive is downloaded and extracted we need to set the correct permissions on the cache and storage directories to avoid
any webserver related errors.

```sh
sudo chmod -R 755 storage/* bootstrap/cache
```

### Update Dependencies

```sh
sudo COMPOSER_ALLOW_SUPERUSER=1 composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
```

> **Info**
>
> Even though composer might tell you that you have outdated dependencies, do **not** run `composer update`!

### Create storage symlinks

```sh
sudo php artisan storage:link
```

### Cache components

```sh
sudo php artisan optimize:clear
sudo php artisan filament:optimize
```

### Update Database

You'll also need to update your database schema. Running the command below
will update the schema and ensure the default eggs we ship are up to date (and add any new ones we might have). Just
remember, _never edit core eggs we ship_! They will be overwritten by this update process.

```sh
sudo php artisan migrate --seed --force
```

### Themes

If you previously had any themes installed you need to manually build the panel assets again:

```sh
yarn install
yarn build
```

### Set Permissions

The last step is to set proper ownership of the files. In most cases this
is `www-data` but can vary from system to system &mdash; sometimes being `nginx`, `caddy`, `apache`, or even `nobody`.

#### NGINX/ Apache/ Caddy

```sh
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/pelican
```

#### Rocky Linux NGINX

```sh
sudo chown -R nginx:nginx /var/www/pelican
```

#### Rocky Linux Apache

```sh
sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www/pelican
```

### Restart Queue Workers

After _every update_ you should restart the queue worker.

```sh
sudo php artisan queue:restart
```

### Exit Maintenance Mode

Now that everything has been updated you need to exit maintenance mode.

```sh
sudo php artisan up
```

---

# Using Redis with the Panel

> Install Redis from its official apt repository and switch an existing Pelican Panel to Redis with the p:redis:setup command.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/redis/

Redis can hold the Panel's cache, sessions and queue instead of the default drivers. This page installs Redis and shows how to switch a Panel that is already installed to it; on a new install you enter the Redis details in the web installer instead.

## Install Redis

To install Redis you first need add their repository.

```sh
sudo apt install -y lsb-release curl gpg
curl -fsSL https://packages.redis.io/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/redis-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/redis-archive-keyring.gpg] https://packages.redis.io/deb $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/redis.list
```

Now you can install Redis by simply running the following commands.

```sh
sudo apt update -y
sudo apt install -y redis-server
```

Also make sure to enable that redis will start on boot. You can do that by running the following command:

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now redis-server
```

## Setup Pelican for Redis

### Use Redis as driver

If you are switching to Redis after installing the Panel you have to run the setup command below.
**You do not have to run this if this is the first time you are installing the Panel. You will provide the redis data via the Web Installer.**

```sh
cd /var/www/pelican
php artisan p:redis:setup
```

---

# Using MySQL or MariaDB with the Panel

> Install MariaDB, create a database and user for the Pelican Panel and switch an existing panel from SQLite to MySQL.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/mysql/

The Panel uses SQLite unless you choose MySQL or MariaDB. This page installs MariaDB, creates a database and user for the Panel, and shows how to switch a Panel that is already installed from SQLite; on a new install you enter the database details in the web installer instead.

## Install MariaDB

MariaDB is a MySQL fork and the preferred MySQL software. Run the following commands to quickly install it.

```sh
curl -sSL https://downloads.mariadb.com/MariaDB/mariadb_repo_setup | sudo bash
sudo apt install -y mariadb-server
```

## Create User & Database

### Logging In

After installing you want to login to the MySQL command line where we will be executing statements to get
things setup. To do so, simply run the command below and provide the Root MySQL account's password that you setup when
installing MySQL. If you do not remember doing this, chances are you can just hit enter as no password is set.

```sh
mysql -u root -p
```

### Creating User

Next, we will create a user called `pelican` and allow logins from localhost which prevents any external connections
to our database. You can also use `%` as a wildcard or enter a numeric IP. We will also set the account password
to `somePassword`.

```sql
CREATE USER 'pelican'@'127.0.0.1' IDENTIFIED BY 'somePassword';
```

### Creating Database

Next, we need to create a database for the panel. In this tutorial we will be naming the database `panel`, but you can
substitute that for whatever name you wish.

```sql
CREATE DATABASE panel;
```

### Assigning Permissions

Finally, we need to tell MySQL that our pelican user should have access to the panel database. To do this, simply
run the command below.

```sql
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON panel.* TO 'pelican'@'127.0.0.1';
```

## Setup Pelican for MySQL

If you are switching to MySQL after installing the Panel you have to run the database setup command below.
**You do not have to run this if this is the first time you are installing the Panel. You will provide the database data via the Web Installer.**

```sh
cd /var/www/pelican
php artisan p:environment:database
```

---

# Artisan Commands

> Reference for Pelican's php artisan commands to manage users, nodes, servers, eggs, plugins, environment settings, migrations and cache.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/artisan/

Pelican's `php artisan` commands manage the Panel from the command line: users, nodes, servers, eggs, plugins, environment settings, migrations and the cache. Run them from the Panel's directory (`/var/www/pelican` on an install without Docker).

This list is still a work in progress: there are many commands, and the layout might change.

Updated: 01/11/2026

## Panel Information

Displays the application, database, email and backup configurations along with the panel version.
```sh
php artisan p:info
```

## User Commands
### Create a User

Creates a user on the system via the CLI.
```sh
php artisan p:user:make [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --email[=EMAIL]
      --username[=USERNAME]
      --password[=PASSWORD]
      --admin[=ADMIN]
      --no-password
  -q, --quiet                Do not output any message
  -V, --version              Display this application version
      --ansi|--no-ansi       Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction       Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Delete a User

Deletes a user from the Panel if no servers are attached to their account.
```sh
php artisan p:user:delete [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --user[=USER]
  -q, --quiet           Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi  Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction  Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Disable 2fa for a single User

Disable two-factor authentication for a specific user in the Panel.
```sh
php artisan p:user:disable2fa [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --email[=EMAIL]   The email of the user to disable 2-Factor for.
  -q, --quiet           Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi  Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction  Do not ask any interactive question

```

## Node Commands
### Create a Node

Creates a new node on the system via the CLI.
```sh
php artisan p:node:make [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --name[=NAME]                                    A name to identify the node.
      --description[=DESCRIPTION]                      A description to identify the node.
      --locationId[=LOCATIONID]                        A valid locationId.
      --fqdn[=FQDN]                                    The domain name (e.g node.example.com) to be used for connecting to the daemon. An IP address may only be used if you are not using SSL for this node.
      --public[=PUBLIC]                                Should the node be public or private? (public=1 / private=0).
      --scheme[=SCHEME]                                Which scheme should be used? (Enable SSL=https / Disable SSL=http).
      --proxy[=PROXY]                                  Is the daemon behind a proxy? (Yes=1 / No=0).
      --maintenance[=MAINTENANCE]                      Should maintenance mode be enabled? (Enable Maintenance mode=1 / Disable Maintenance mode=0).
      --maxMemory[=MAXMEMORY]                          Set the max memory amount.
      --overallocateMemory[=OVERALLOCATEMEMORY]        Enter the amount of ram to overallocate (% or -1 to overallocate the maximum).
      --maxDisk[=MAXDISK]                              Set the max disk amount.
      --overallocateDisk[=OVERALLOCATEDISK]            Enter the amount of disk to overallocate (% or -1 to overallocate the maximum).
      --maxCpu[=MAXCPU]                                Set the max cpu amount.
      --overallocateCpu[=OVERALLOCATECPU]              Enter the amount of cpu to overallocate (% or -1 to overallocate the maximum).
      --uploadSize[=UPLOADSIZE]                        Enter the maximum upload filesize.
      --daemonListeningPort[=DAEMONLISTENINGPORT]      Enter the daemon listening port.
      --daemonConnectingPort[=DAEMONCONNECTINGPORT]    Enter the daemon connecting port.
      --daemonSFTPPort[=DAEMONSFTPPORT]                Enter the daemon SFTP listening port.
      --daemonSFTPAlias[=DAEMONSFTPALIAS]              Enter the daemon SFTP alias.
      --daemonBase[=DAEMONBASE]                        Enter the base folder.
  -q, --quiet                                          Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi                                 Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction                                 Do not ask any interactive question
```

### List Nodes

Lists all nodes with their ID, UUID, name and host.
```sh
php artisan p:node:list [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --format[=FORMAT]  The output format: "text" or "json". [default: "text"]
  -q, --quiet            Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi   Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction   Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Node Configuration

Displays the Wings configuration for the specified node.
```sh
php artisan p:node:configuration [options] <node>
```

```sh
Arguments:
  node                   The ID or UUID of the node to return the configuration for.

Options:
      --format[=FORMAT]  The output format. Options are "yaml" and "json". [default: "yaml"]
  -q, --quiet            Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi   Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction   Do not ask any interactive question
```

## Server Commands
### Bulk Power Actions

Perform bulk power management on large groupings of servers or nodes at once.
```sh
php artisan p:server:bulk-power [options] <action>
```

```sh
Arguments:
  action                 The action to perform (start, stop, restart, kill)

Options:
      --servers[=SERVERS]  A comma separated list of servers.
      --nodes[=NODES]      A comma separated list of nodes.
  -q, --quiet              Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi     Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction     Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Process Schedules

Process schedules in the database and determine which are ready to run. This runs every minute via the scheduler.
```sh
php artisan p:schedule:process
```

## Egg Commands
### Check for Egg Updates

Compares each egg against its update URL and reports whether it is up to date. Eggs without an update URL are skipped. This runs daily via the scheduler.
```sh
php artisan p:egg:check-updates
```

### Update Egg Index

Refreshes the cached index of available eggs from the Pelican CDN. This runs daily via the scheduler.
```sh
php artisan p:egg:update-index
```

### Normalize an Egg

Upgrades an egg json/yaml file to the latest format as yaml.
```sh
php artisan p:egg:normalize [options] <file>
```

```sh
Arguments:
  file                   Path to the egg json/yaml file.

Options:
      --delete-original  Delete the original file after converting.
  -q, --quiet            Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi   Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction   Do not ask any interactive question
```

## Plugin Commands
### List Plugins

List all installed plugins.
```sh
php artisan p:plugin:list
```

### Create a Plugin

Create a new plugin.
```sh
php artisan p:plugin:make [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --name[=NAME]
      --author[=AUTHOR]
      --description[=DESCRIPTION]
      --category[=CATEGORY]
      --url[=URL]
      --updateUrl[=UPDATEURL]
      --panels[=PANELS]
      --panelVersion[=PANELVERSION]
  -q, --quiet                    Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi           Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction           Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Install a Plugin

Installs and enables a plugin. If no `id` is given you will be asked to choose one.
```sh
php artisan p:plugin:install [<id>]
```

### Update a Plugin

Updates a plugin, if an update is available.
```sh
php artisan p:plugin:update [<id>]
```

### Disable a Plugin

Disables a plugin.
```sh
php artisan p:plugin:disable [<id>]
```

### Uninstall a Plugin

Uninstalls a plugin.
```sh
php artisan p:plugin:uninstall [options] [<id>]
```

```sh
Options:
      --delete           Delete the plugin files
  -q, --quiet            Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi   Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction   Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Install Plugin Composer Packages

Makes sure the needed composer packages for all installed plugins are available.
```sh
php artisan p:plugin:composer
```

## Maintenance Commands
### Prune Docker Images

Clean up all dangling docker images to clear up disk space. If no node ID is given, all nodes are cleaned. This runs daily via the scheduler.
```sh
php artisan p:maintenance:prune-images [<node>]
```

### Prune Orphaned Backups

Marks all backups older than "n" minutes that have not yet completed as being failed. Defaults to the `backups.prune_age` config value (360 minutes).
```sh
php artisan p:maintenance:prune-backups [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --prune-age[=PRUNE-AGE]  Age in minutes after which an uncompleted backup is marked as failed.
  -q, --quiet                  Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi         Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction         Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Clean Service Backup Files

Clean orphaned .bak files created when modifying services. This runs daily via the scheduler.
```sh
php artisan p:maintenance:clean-service-backups
```

### Fix Database Grants

Re-issues the grants of all server databases so that their names are no longer used as wildcard patterns.
```sh
php artisan p:maintenance:fix-database-grants
```

## Migrations
### Migration Command
```sh
php artisan migrate [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --database[=DATABASE]        The database connection to use
      --force                      Force the operation to run when in production
      --path[=PATH]                The path(s) to the migrations files to be executed (multiple values allowed)
      --realpath                   Indicate any provided migration file paths are pre-resolved absolute paths
      --schema-path[=SCHEMA-PATH]  The path to a schema dump file
      --pretend                    Dump the SQL queries that would be run
      --seed                       Indicates if the seed task should be re-run
      --seeder[=SEEDER]            The class name of the root seeder
      --step                       Force the migrations to be run so they can be rolled back individually
      --graceful                   Return a successful exit code even if an error occurs
      --isolated[=ISOLATED]        Do not run the command if another instance of the command is already running [default: false]
  -q, --quiet                      Do not output any message
      --ansi|--no-ansi       Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction             Do not ask any interactive question
```
### Running Migations
```sh
php artisan migrate
```

### Rollback previous Migration
```sh
php artisan migrate:rollback [options]
```

```sh
Options:
      --database[=DATABASE]  The database connection to use
      --force                Force the operation to run when in production
      --path[=PATH]          The path(s) to the migrations files to be executed (multiple values allowed)
      --realpath             Indicate any provided migration file paths are pre-resolved absolute paths
      --pretend              Dump the SQL queries that would be run
      --step[=STEP]          The number of migrations to be reverted
      --batch=BATCH          The batch of migrations (identified by their batch number) to be reverted
      --ansi|--no-ansi       Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction       Do not ask any interactive question
```

### Check Migration Status
```sh
php artisan migrate:status [options]
```
```sh
Options:
      --database[=DATABASE]  The database connection to use
      --pending[=PENDING]    Only list pending migrations [default: false]
      --path[=PATH]          The path(s) to the migrations files to use (multiple values allowed)
      --realpath             Indicate any provided migration file paths are pre-resolved absolute paths
      --ansi|--no-ansi       Force (or disable --no-ansi) ANSI output
  -n, --no-interaction       Do not ask any interactive question
```
Providing no extra options, `php artisan migrate:status`, You should see an output similar to the below
```sh
  Migration name .............................................................................. Batch / Status
  2016_01_23_195641_add_allocations_table ............................................................ [1] Ran
  2016_01_23_195851_add_api_keys ..................................................................... [1] Ran
  ...
  ...
  2024_07_12_095213_fix_missing_sqlite_foreign_keys .................................................. [1] Ran
  2024_08_13_171337_fix_allocation_server_foreign_key ................................................ [2] Ran
```
If any show `PENDING` or `FAILED`. Open a support thread on our discord for further assistance.

## Clearing Cache

The below commands are helpful if you need to clear the config or application cache.

```sh
php artisan cache:clear # Clears application cache
```
```sh
php artisan config:clear # Clears configuration cache
```


> **Note**
>
> `php artisan config:cache` is disabled in Pelican, and `php artisan optimize` skips config caching. Caching the config would stop plugin config files (`/plugins/config/*.php`) from loading.
