# Deploying with Podman

> Run the Pelican Panel's Docker image with rootless Podman on Fedora, RHEL or Alma/Rocky Linux, using a Quadlet so systemd manages the container.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/podman/

This guide runs the panel's [Docker image](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/) with **rootless Podman** on Fedora, RHEL, or Alma/Rocky Linux, using a **Quadlet** so systemd manages the container. Like the Docker guide, it uses SQLite and serves the panel over plain HTTP on port 80.

## Prerequisites

* **OS:** Fedora, RHEL 9+, or Alma/Rocky Linux 9+ with SELinux enforcing.
* **Packages:** `podman` 5 or newer (`sudo dnf install podman`).
* A regular (non-root) user to run the panel. The commands below use `your-user`; replace it with that user's name.

> **Info**
>
> Data is stored in Podman named volumes (`pelican-data` and `pelican-logs`), under `~/.local/share/containers/storage/volumes`. Podman applies the correct SELinux labels to these automatically.

## 1. Allow Rootless Containers to Use Port 80

Unprivileged users can't bind ports below 1024 by default. Lower that limit to 80:

```sh
echo 'net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=80' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/podman-ports.conf
sudo sysctl --system
```

## 2. Create the Pod

Create the directories:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/pelican ~/.config/containers/systemd
```

Create the pod definition. Set `APP_URL` to the address users will visit.

```yaml title="~/pelican/pelican.yaml"
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pelican
  annotations:
    # Optional: lets `podman auto-update` pull new panel images
    io.containers.autoupdate: registry
spec:
  securityContext:
    sysctls:
      # The panel's web server doesn't run as root, so let it listen on port 80 inside the pod
      - name: net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start
        value: "0"
  containers:
    - name: panel
      image: ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          hostPort: 80
      volumeMounts:
        - name: pelican-data
          mountPath: /pelican-data
        - name: pelican-logs
          mountPath: /var/www/html/storage/logs
      env:
        - name: XDG_DATA_HOME
          value: /pelican-data
        - name: APP_URL
          value: "http://YOUR_SERVER_IP"
  volumes:
    - name: pelican-data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: pelican-data
    - name: pelican-logs
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: pelican-logs
```

Then create the Quadlet, which tells systemd to run that pod:

```ini title="~/.config/containers/systemd/pelican.kube"
[Unit]
Description=Pelican Panel
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Kube]
Yaml=%h/pelican/pelican.yaml
# Give the pod its own address so the panel can reach Wings and its own APP_URL on this host
Network=pasta:-a,10.0.2.15,-n,24,-g,10.0.2.2

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

> **Note**
>
> Without the `Network=` line, Podman gives the pod the host's IP address. The panel then can't reach anything on the host by that IP, such as Wings running on the same server.

## 3. Start the Panel

Let the panel keep running when you are logged out, then start it:

```sh
loginctl enable-linger $USER
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user start pelican.service
```

Check that it is running and view its logs:

```sh
systemctl --user status pelican.service
podman logs -f pelican-panel
```

### Back Up Your Encryption Key

The first time the container starts, it generates an `APP_KEY`, which is used as an encryption key. Save a copy in a secure place in case you need it later:

```sh
podman exec pelican-panel grep APP_KEY /pelican-data/.env
```

### Installing

Open the installer in your browser at `http://YOUR_SERVER_IP/installer` to finish setting up the panel.

## Optional Configuration

### HTTPS and Reverse Proxies

The image supports the same `BEHIND_PROXY`, `LE_EMAIL` and `TRUSTED_PROXIES` environment variables as the [Docker deployment](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#reverse-proxy-configuration). Add them under `env:` in `pelican.yaml`. If the panel serves HTTPS itself, also publish port 443 (`containerPort: 443`, `hostPort: 443`).

### Upload Limit

The default file upload limit is 2MB. To raise it, copy the image's Caddyfile and edit it as shown in the [Docker guide](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/):

```sh
podman run --rm --entrypoint cat ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest /etc/caddy/Caddyfile > ~/pelican/Caddyfile
```

Allow containers to read it under SELinux (`semanage` is in the `policycoreutils-python-utils` package):

```sh
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t container_file_t "/home/your-user/pelican/Caddyfile"
sudo restorecon -v ~/pelican/Caddyfile
```

Then mount it in `pelican.yaml`. Add this under the panel's `volumeMounts`:

```yaml
        - name: caddyfile
          mountPath: /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
```

And add this under `volumes` (`hostPath` must be an absolute path):

```yaml
    - name: caddyfile
      hostPath:
        path: /home/your-user/pelican/Caddyfile
        type: File
```

Restart the panel with `systemctl --user restart pelican.service`.

### Automatic Updates

The `io.containers.autoupdate` annotation lets Podman update the panel image. Enable the timer to check daily:

```sh
systemctl --user enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
```

## Managing Data

List the volumes, and find where their data is stored for backups:

```sh
podman volume ls
podman volume inspect pelican-data
```

> **Danger**
>
> `podman volume rm pelican-data` permanently deletes the panel's data, including the SQLite database and your encryption key.

---

# Cloudflare Tunnel

> Serve the Docker install of the Pelican Panel over HTTPS through a Cloudflare Tunnel, without opening any inbound ports on the host, and keep Wings reachable.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/cloudflare-tunnel/

A [Cloudflare Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/connections/connect-networks/) lets you serve the panel over HTTPS without opening any inbound ports on your host. A small `cloudflared` container makes an outbound connection to Cloudflare, and Cloudflare forwards requests for your hostname down that connection to the panel.

This guide builds on the [Docker](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/) installation. Read that page first, as the steps for backing up your encryption key, installing, and stopping the panel are the same.

> **Info**
>
> This page only covers the panel. Wings still needs to be reachable by your users' browsers and by the panel, see [Wings](#wings) below.

## Prerequisites

- Docker CE with Docker Compose v2 (see the [Docker installation guide](https://pelican.dev/docs/getting-started/))
- A domain whose DNS is managed by Cloudflare
- A Cloudflare Zero Trust account (the free plan is enough)

## Create the Tunnel

1. Open the [Cloudflare dashboard](https://dash.cloudflare.com/) and go to **Networking** → **Tunnels**. (In the older Zero Trust dashboard this is **Networks** → **Tunnels**.)
2. Click **Create a tunnel**, choose **Cloudflared**, give it a name (e.g. `pelican`) and save it.
3. On the install screen, copy the token from the shown command (the long string after `--token`). You do not need to install anything on the host, Docker will run `cloudflared` for you.
4. Under **Routes**, click **Add route** and choose **Published application** (called a public hostname in older versions of the dashboard):
    - **Subdomain** and **Domain**: the hostname you want the panel on, e.g. `panel.example.com`
    - **Service Type**: `HTTP`
    - **URL**: `panel:80`

`panel:80` is the panel container's name and internal port. Cloudflare creates the DNS record for the hostname automatically.

## Create compose.yml

Create a directory for the panel, and in it a `.env` file holding your tunnel token. Docker Compose reads this file automatically, which keeps the token out of `compose.yml`.

```sh title=".env"
TUNNEL_TOKEN=paste-your-tunnel-token-here
```

Then create `compose.yml` next to it:

```yml title="compose.yml"
services:
  panel:
    image: ghcr.io/pelican/panel:latest
    restart: always
    networks:
      - default
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"
    volumes:
      - pelican-data:/pelican-data
      - pelican-logs:/var/www/html/storage/logs
    environment:
      XDG_DATA_HOME: /pelican-data
      APP_URL: "https://panel.example.com"
      ADMIN_EMAIL: "USEYOUROWNEMAILHERE@example.com"
      BEHIND_PROXY: "true"
      TRUSTED_PROXIES: "172.20.0.0/16"

  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    restart: always
    networks:
      - default
    command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run
    environment:
      TUNNEL_TOKEN: ${TUNNEL_TOKEN}

volumes:
  pelican-data:
  pelican-logs:

networks:
  default:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.20.0.0/16
```

Compared to the standard Docker setup:

- There is no `ports:` section. Nothing is published on the host, all traffic arrives through the tunnel.
- `APP_URL` is the public `https://` hostname from the tunnel.
- `BEHIND_PROXY` makes the panel listen on plain HTTP port 80 and skip Let's Encrypt, since Cloudflare handles TLS (SSL). See [Reverse Proxy Configuration](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#reverse-proxy-configuration).
- `TRUSTED_PROXIES` is the Docker network's subnet, so the panel trusts the forwarded headers from the `cloudflared` container. If you change the subnet, change both.

## Start the Panel

```sh
docker compose up -d
```

Check that the tunnel connected:

```sh
docker compose logs cloudflared
```

You should see `Registered tunnel connection`, and the tunnel should show as **Healthy** in the Cloudflare dashboard.

Now [back up your encryption key](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#back-up-your-encryption-key) and open `https://panel.example.com/installer` to [finish installing](https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/install/#installing).

## Wings

Wings cannot share the panel's tunnel hostname. The panel talks to Wings, and your users' browsers open a websocket directly to Wings for the console, so the node's FQDN must be reachable on its own. You can either:

- Expose Wings directly, optionally through the Cloudflare proxy. See [Enabling Cloudflare proxy](https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/optional-config/#enabling-cloudflare-proxy).
- Route a second public hostname on a tunnel to Wings. When creating the node, choose **HTTPS with (reverse) proxy**, which sets the connection port to `443` and the listen port to `8080`, and point the tunnel's service at `http://<wings host>:8080`.

Either way, keep in mind:

- SFTP (port `2022` by default) is plain TCP and does not work through an HTTP tunnel. Expose it directly if you need it.
- Cloudflare limits request body size by plan (100 MB on Free and Pro). Uploads through a proxied Wings hostname larger than that will fail.
- Run Wings in its own compose project rather than adding it to this one, so a not-yet-configured Wings does not restart in a loop alongside the panel.

## Troubleshooting

**The tunnel is healthy but the site returns a 502 or "Unable to reach origin service"**
- Check the public hostname's URL is `panel:80` (not `localhost:80`) and the type is `HTTP`.
- Check the panel container is running with `docker compose ps`. On first start, it may still be applying migrations, see `docker compose logs panel`.

**The site redirects in a loop, or the panel exits complaining about a Let's Encrypt email**
- `BEHIND_PROXY` is not set to `"true"`.

**Pages load but links, assets or logins use the wrong address**
- `APP_URL` must match the tunnel hostname exactly, including `https://`.

**File uploads fail**
- `TRUSTED_PROXIES` must cover the subnet the `cloudflared` container is on.

## Security

- Do not commit `.env`. Anyone with the tunnel token can run your tunnel.
- Consider putting a [Cloudflare Access](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/applications/configure-apps/self-hosted-public-app/) policy in front of the panel, at least until the installer has been completed. Wings calls the panel's API at `/api/remote` and cannot complete an Access login, so before connecting Wings either remove the policy or add a Bypass policy for `panel.example.com/api/remote`.

---

# Panel API documentation

> Find the built-in API docs for your Pelican Panel at /docs/api, covering the Application API and the Client API.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/api-docs/

The docs for the Pelican API can be found by going to `/docs/api` on your panel.

> **Warning: Sign in before accessing the API docs**
>
> You must sign in on the login page **before** accessing the docs.

For example:
```bash
https://yourpaneladdress.com/docs/api
```

You can also visit the docs on the demo instance [here](https://demo.pelican.dev/docs/api).

There are two APIs you can interact with. The first is the Application API. The application API is used more for adjusting the server configuration.
The second is the client API. This API is more for interacting with the features that users normally interact with.

---

# Panel Plugins: install, create and publish

> Install, update and uninstall Pelican Panel plugins, and create and publish your own with Filament resources, translations, settings and permissions.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/panel/advanced/plugins/

Plugins allow you to add new functionality to the panel without modifying any panel core files.

> **Warning**
>
> The plugin system is still in development and features might be missing!

## Install a Plugin

### Via Panel Frontend

Use the Import button on the plugin list to upload a plugin. After the import is done, use the Install button to complete the installation.

Plugin installs run in the background so it might take a few seconds. If a plugin isn't installing [check your queue worker configuration](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/troubleshooting/#schedules-not-running).

### Manually

Move the plugin folder to `plugins` inside your panel directory (`/var/www/pelican/plugins` by default). Then run `php artisan p:plugin:install` inside your panel directory and select the new plugin.

> **Info: Need some plugins?**
>
> You can find various official and third party plugins on the [Hub plugin marketplace](https://hub.pelican.dev/plugins)!
> Also check out our [Plugins repo](https://github.com/pelican/plugins)! It contains free and open source plugins created by the Pelican team.

## Update a Plugin

For one-click updates to work the plugin needs to have a [update url](#update-url) set. Otherwise you need to manually update the plugin files.

### Via Panel Frontend

The panel will automatically check for plugins updates when visiting the plugin list. If an update is available you can use the Update button to download and install the update.

Plugin updates run in the background so it might take a few seconds. If a plugin isn't updating [check your queue worker configuration](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/troubleshooting/#schedules-not-running).

### Manually

Run `php artisan p:plugin:update` inside your panel directory (`/var/www/pelican` by default) and select the plugin you want to update.

## Uninstall a Plugin

### Via Panel Frontend

Use the Uninstall button on the plugin list.

Plugin uninstalls run in the background so it might take a few seconds. If a plugin isn't uninstalling [check your queue worker configuration](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/troubleshooting/#schedules-not-running).

### Manually

Run `php artisan p:plugin:uninstall` inside your panel directory (`/var/www/pelican` by default) and select the plugin you want to uninstall.

## Create a Plugin

> **Danger**
>
> You **need** at least basic [PHP](https://php.net), [Laravel](https://laravel.com) and [Filament](https://filamentphp.com) knowledge to create plugins!

Run `php artisan p:plugin:make` inside your panel directory (`/var/www/pelican` by default) to create the basic files and folders for your new plugin. This will create the `plugin.json`, the main plugin file, a config file and a service provider.

> **Info: Need help?**
>
> Visit our [Discord](https://discord.gg/pelican-panel) if you need any help when creating plugins!

### Plugin Structure

The two most important files of your plugin are the `plugin.json` (which contains general information like name, version etc.) and the main plugin file. (where you can load Filament resources, pages etc.)
While the `plugin.json` is in the root of your plugin folder, the main plugin file is in `src`.

In general, the plugin folder tries to mimic the structure of a normal Laravel/FilamentPHP project. For example, translations go into `lang` and migrations are in `database/migrations`.
Everything is auto-discovered and service providers, artisan commands, migrations etc. are automatically registered.

The only exception to a normal Laravel project is the `app` folder, it is called `src` instead. Besides that, is still follows the same sub-structure, e.g. models go in `src/Models` and service providers are in `src/Providers`.

> **Info**
>
> The plugin id and the plugin root folder name need to match!

#### plugin.json

Most of the fields inside the `plugin.json` are generated when running the [artisan command](#create-a-plugin).

| Field             | Required | Description                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| id                | Yes      | Unique identifier of the plugin. Has to match with the plugin root folder name!                                                                               |
| name              | Yes      | Display name of the plugin.                                                                                                                                   |
| author            | Yes      | Display name of the plugin creator.                                                                                                                           |
| version           | No       | Version of the plugin. Ideally, this should follow [semantic versioning](https://semver.org/). When not set it will assume version 1.0.0.                     |
| description       | No       | Short description of the plugin.                                                                                                                              |
| category          | Yes      | Either `plugin`, `theme` or `language`.                                                                                                                       |
| update_url        | No       | URL that will be fetched when checking for updates. See [below](#update-url) for more information.                                                            |
| namespace         | Yes      | The php namespace for the plugin files.                                                                                                                       |
| class             | Yes      | The name of the plugin main class.                                                                                                                            |
| panels            | No       | Array of [FilamentPHP panel](#filament-panels) ids the plugin should be loaded on. When not set the plugin will be loaded on all panels.                      |
| panel_version     | No       | The panel version required for the plugin. See [below](#panel-version) for more information.                                                                  |
| api_version       | No       | The plugin api version the plugin targets. When not set, version 1 is assumed. See [below](#api-version) for more information.                                |
| composer_packages | No       | Array of additional composer packages. Key is the package name and value is the version. See [below](#additional-composer-dependencies) for more information. |

> **Info**
>
> You can ignore the `meta` fields. Those are used internally to keep track of the plugin status and load order.

#### Update URL

In your `plugin.json` you can specify an `update_url` that is fetched when checking for plugin updates.
When not set, there will be no update checking for the plugin.

It needs to point directly to a json file with the following format:

```json title="update.json"
{
    "panel_version_1": {
        "version": "1.0.0",
        "download_url": "..."
    },
    "panel_version_2": {
        "version": "1.1.0",
        "download_url": "..."
    }
}
```

If you don't have panel-version-specific plugin versions, you can also use `*` as panel version wildcard:

```json title="update.json"
{
    "*": {
        "version": "1.1.0",
        "download_url": "..."
    }
}
```

You can also mix the wildcard with real panel versions. This way the wildcard will be used as fallback when the users panel version isn't specified in the update json.

Example:

```json title="update.json"
{
    "panel_version_1": {
        "version": "1.0.0",
        "download_url": "..."
    },
    "*": {
        "version": "1.1.0",
        "download_url": "..."
    }
}
```

#### Additional composer dependencies

If you need additional composer packages as dependency for your plugin, you can add the package name to the `composer_packages` array in your `plugin.json`.

Example:

```json
"composer_packages": {
    "package/one": "^1.0",
    "package/two": "^1.0"
}
```

#### Panel version

In your `plugin.json` you can specify a `panel_version` that is used for compatibility checks.
When not set, the plugin will be loaded regardless of the panel version.

You can add a `^` in front of the version to turn the strict constraint into a range with the same semantics as composer's caret, e.g. `1.2.0` means "_only_ version 1.2.0" while `^1.2.0` means "version 1.2.0 or higher, but below 2.0.0". For `0.x` constraints the range caps at the next minor instead, e.g. `^0.3` allows 0.3.0 up to (but not including) 0.4.0, and `0.0.x` constraints cap at the next patch, e.g. `^0.0.3` only allows 0.0.3.

#### Api version

In your `plugin.json` you can specify an `api_version` that declares which version of the plugin api your plugin targets. The current plugin api version is **1**.

When not set, version 1 is assumed and the plugin list shows a small warning under the plugin status. If a plugin declares a newer api version than the panel supports, the panel refuses to load it and marks it as incompatible. This way a future breaking change to the plugin api can't take down a panel that still runs older plugins.

### Filament Resources

To simply register Filament resources, pages or widgets you can add the following snippet to the `register` function in your main plugin file:

```php
$id = str($panel->getId())->title();

$panel->discoverPages(plugin_path($this->getId(), "src/Filament/$id/Pages"), "<namespace>\\Filament\\$id\\Pages");
$panel->discoverResources(plugin_path($this->getId(), "src/Filament/$id/Resources"), "<namespace>\\Filament\\$id\\Resources");
$panel->discoverWidgets(plugin_path($this->getId(), "src/Filament/$id/Widgets"), "<namespace>\\Filament\\$id\\Widgets");
```

Make sure to replace `<namespace>` with your actual namespace.

### Filament Panels

By default there are three Filament panels:

1. `admin` (Admin Area)
2. `app` (Server list)
3. `server` (Client Area, with `Server` model as [tenant](https://filamentphp.com/docs/4.x/users/tenancy))

#### App panel

The `app` panel is solely used for the server list and has no navigation.
If you want to expand the `app` panel, you can re-enable the navigation by adding the following snippet to the `register` function in your main plugin file:

```php
if ($panel->getId() === 'app') {
    // Optional: "Embed" the server list. This will add a Servers navigation item for the server list.
    // ServerResource::embedServerList();

    // Re-enable navigation
    $panel->navigation(true);

    // By default the topbar is always used. With proper navigation we want to conditionally enable it based on the users customization
    $panel->topbar(function () {
        $navigationType = user()?->getCustomization(CustomizationKey::TopNavigation);

        return $navigationType === 'topbar' || $navigationType === 'mixed' || $navigationType === true;
    });

    // Rebuild component cache
    $panel->clearCachedComponents();
}
```

### Translations

Normally, translations will be registered under the namespace of your plugin.
This means you need to prefix translation keys with your plugin id when using `trans()`, e.g. `trans('myplugin::strings.test')` would look for `test` inside `plugins/myplugin/lang/strings.php`.

If your plugin adds new default languages to the panel you need to set the plugin category to `language`. This way translations will be registered without any namespace.

### Views

Views are automatically registered under the namespace of your plugin.
This means you need to prefix view-strings with your plugin id, e.g. `myplugin::my-view` would look for `plugins/myplugin/resources/views/my-view.blade.php`.

### Seeder

If present, a seeder with the name of your plugin will be automatically registered. It needs to be named `<plugin name>Seeder` (e.g. `MyPluginSeeder`) and put inside your plugins `database/Seeder` folder, e.g. `plugins/myplugin/database/Seeder/MyPluginSeeder.php`.
This seeder will be automatically called when a user installs the plugin or when seeders are run in general, e.g. when using `php artisan db:seed` or `php artisan migrate --seed`.

### Routes

Routes need to be registered in a `RouteServiceProvider`. Example:

```php
use Illuminate\Foundation\Support\Providers\RouteServiceProvider;

class MyPluginRoutesProvider extends RouteServiceProvider
{
    public function boot(): void
    {
        $this->routes(function () {
            // Single new endpoint with Controller
            Route::get('test', [TestController::class, 'test'])->name('my-plugin.test');

            // Load routes from file
            Route::prefix('/my-plugin')->group(plugin_path('my-plugin', 'routes/web.php'));

            // Add routes from file to existing client api
            Route::middleware(['api', 'client-api', 'throttle:api.client'])
                ->prefix('/api/client')
                ->scopeBindings()
                ->group(plugin_path('my-plugin', 'routes/api-client.php'));
        });
    }
}
```

### Plugin Settings

Your main plugin class can implement the `HasPluginSettings` interface to conveniently add a settings page to your plugin.
The settings page can be accessed on the plugin list on the panel. Your plugin needs to provide the form, the form data and how the data should be saved.

If you want to save the settings in the `.env` file you can use the `EnvironmentWriterTrait`. Example:

```php
use EnvironmentWriterTrait;

public function getSettingsFormData(): array
{
    return config('myplugin');
}

public function getSettingsForm(): array
{
    return [
        TextInput::make('test_input')
            ->required(),
        Toggle::make('test_toggle')
            ->inline(false),
    ];
}

public function saveSettings(array $data): void
{
    $this->writeToEnvironment([
        'MYPLUGIN_TEST_INPUT' => $data['test_input'],
        'MYPLUGIN_TEST_TOGGLE' => $data['test_toggle'],
    ]);

    Notification::make()
        ->title('Settings saved')
        ->success()
        ->send();
}
```

> **Info: Naming Conventions**
>
> When adding new environment variables make sure to prefix them with your plugin id, e.g. `MYPLUGIN_TEST_INPUT` and not just `TEST_INPUT`.

### Modify existing resources

Most of the default panel resources and pages have static methods to register custom classes or to change existing ones. You can call these static methods inside the `register` function of a service provider.

Examples:

```php title="MyPluginProvider.php"
public function register(): void
{
    // Add new relation manager to UserResource
    UserResource::registerCustomRelations(MyCustomRelationManager::class);

    // Add new widget to Console page
    Console::registerCustomWidgets(ConsoleWidgetPosition::AboveConsole, [MyCustomWidget::class]);

    // Add new header action to Server list page
    ListServers::registerCustomHeaderActions(HeaderActionPosition::Before, MyCustomAction::make());
}
```

For more information you can check the ["CanModify" and "CanCustomize" traits in `./app/Traits/Filament`](https://github.com/pelican/panel/tree/main/app/Traits/Filament).

### Add new permissions

#### Admin Roles

To add new admin role permissions you can use `Role::registerCustomPermissions` and `Role::registerCustomDefaultPermissions`.

You can call these static methods inside the `register` function of a service provider. Examples:

```php title="MyPluginProvider.php"
public function register(): void
{
    // Register default permissions: viewList, view, create, update, delete
    Role::registerCustomDefaultPermissions('myModel');

    // Register custom permissions
    Role::registerCustomPermissions([
        'myModel' => [
            'customPerm1',
            'customPerm2'
        ]
    ]);

    // Optionally, register an icon for a custom model
    Role::registerCustomModelIcon('myModel', 'tabler-star');

    // You can also add new permissions to existing models
    Role::registerCustomPermissions([
        'server' => [
            'custom',
        ]
    ]);
}
```

#### Subuser

To add new subuser permissions you can use `Subuser::registerCustomPermissions`.

You can call this static method inside the `register` function of a service provider. Examples:

```php title="MyPluginProvider.php"
public function register(): void
{
    // Register new subuser permissions (call with icon and hidden param)
    Subuser::registerCustomPermissions('custom', ['customPerm1', 'customPerm2'], 'tabler-star', false);

    // You can also add new permissions to existing permission groups (call without icon and hidden param)
    Subuser::registerCustomPermissions('console', ['custom']);
}
```

## Compatibility Policy

The plugin api follows the panel's [semantic versioning](https://semver.org/). The stable surface plugins can rely on consists of:

- The `plugin.json` schema documented on this page
- The `HasPluginSettings` interface
- Automatic discovery and registration of service providers, artisan commands, migrations, views, translations and seeders as described above
- The `panel_version` compatibility semantics (strict and `^` range constraints)
- The handling of `composer_packages`

Breaking changes to this surface only happen with a new panel major version, and deprecations are announced at least one minor version ahead. The `api_version` field exists so the panel can detect plugins that target a newer, incompatible plugin api.

Anything not listed above, in particular the panel's internal services, models, and Filament internals, can change in any release. The static registration hooks documented on this page (custom permissions, resource modification, etc.) are kept working on a best-effort basis.

## Publish a Plugin

> **Tip**
>
> If possible, please make your plugins open source. Open plugins help others learn from them and help us improve the plugin system!

To publish a plugin you only need to do two things:

1. Open your `plugin.json` and remove the `meta` part.
2. Zip up your whole plugin folder.

And that's it! Now you can take the zip file and share it with the world!

> **Info: Marketplace**
>
> Publish your plugins on the [Hub plugin marketplcae](https://hub.pelican.dev/plugins)! This will allow users to easily install or download your plugin.
> You can also share them in the `#share-plugins` channel in our [Discord](https://discord.gg/pelican-panel).

> **Info: License**
>
> You can license your plugin code under whatever license you want. You do not have to use the same license as the panel!
> You also don't have to open source your plugin code. But if you do want to open source it we recommend [MIT](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/mit) or [GPL v3](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/gpl-3.0) as license.

---

# Installing Wings

> Install Wings on a Linux host with Docker, configure it from a node in the Panel and run it as a systemd service.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/install/

Wings is the service that runs your game servers on each machine (a node), in Docker containers. This page installs Wings on a Linux host, connects it to a node you create in the Panel and keeps it running with systemd.

> **Warning**
>
> This software will not work on Windows operating systems.

> **Tip**
>
> It is always recommended to keep the server files on a separate partition.
> This prevents the root partition from filling and causing the host to crash, potentially becoming unbootable.

## Supported Systems

The following is a list of supported operating systems. Please be aware that this is not an exhaustive list,
there is a high probability that you can run the software on other Linux distributions without much effort.
You are responsible for determining which packages may be necessary on those systems. There is also a very
high probability that new releases of the supported OSes below will work just fine, you are not restricted to
only the versions listed below.

This documentation assumes a Debian/Ubuntu based OS with apt as package manager.

| Operating System | Version  | Supported |
|:----------------:|:--------:|:---------:|
| **Ubuntu**       | 22.04    |     ✅︎︎    |
|                  | 24.04    |     ✅︎    |
|                  | 26.04    |     ✅︎    |
| **Debian**       | 11       |     ✅︎    |
|                  | 12       |     ✅︎    |
|                  | 13       |     ✅︎    |
| **Alma Linux**   | 8        |     ✅︎    |
|                  | 9        |     ✅︎    |
|                  | 10       |     ✅︎    |
| **Rocky Linux**  | 8        |     ✅︎    |
|                  | 9        |     ✅︎    |
|                  | 10       |     ✅︎    |
| **CentOS**       | 10       |     ✅︎    |

## System Requirements

> **Warning**
>
> Please be aware that some hosts install a modified kernel that does not support some docker features required for Wings to operate correctly. Please
> check your kernel by running `uname -r`. If your kernel ends in `-xxxx-grs-ipv6-64` or `-xxxx-mod-std-ipv6-64` you're
> probably using a non-supported kernel. You should contact your host, and request a non-modified kernel.

To run Wings, you will need a Linux system capable of running Docker containers. Most VPS and almost all
dedicated servers should be capable of running Docker, but there are edge cases.

When your provider uses `Virtuozzo`, `OpenVZ` (or `OVZ`), or `LXC` virtualization, you will most likely be unable to
run Wings. Some providers have made the necessary changes for nested virtualization to support Docker. Ask your provider's support team to make sure. KVM is guaranteed to work.

The easiest way to check is to type `systemd-detect-virt`.
If the result doesn't contain `OpenVZ` or`LXC`, it should be fine. The result of `none` will appear when running dedicated hardware without any virtualization.

Should that not work for some reason, or you're still unsure, you can also run the command below.

```sh
sudo dmidecode -s system-manufacturer
```

### Installing Docker
Wings requires Docker CE. For full instructions on installing and configuring Docker, see [Getting Started](https://pelican.dev/docs/getting-started/).

For a quick install of Docker CE, you can use the command below:

```sh
curl -sSL https://get.docker.com/ | CHANNEL=stable sudo sh
```

### Installing Wings

The first step for installing Wings is to ensure we have the required directory structure setup. To do so,
run the commands below, which will create the base directory and download the wings executable.

```sh
sudo mkdir -p /etc/pelican /var/run/wings
sudo curl -L -o /usr/local/bin/wings "https://github.com/pelican/wings/releases/latest/download/wings_linux_$([[ "$(uname -m)" == "x86_64" ]] && echo "amd64" || echo "arm64")"
sudo chmod u+x /usr/local/bin/wings
```

### Configure

Once you have installed Wings and the required components, the next step is to create a node on your installed Panel.
Go to your Panel administrative view, select Nodes from the sidebar, and on the right side click Create New button.

After you have created a node, click on it and there will be a tab called Configuration.
Copy the code block content, create a new file at `/etc/pelican/config.yml`, paste the content into it and save.

Alternatively, you can click on the Auto Deploy Command button, copy the sh command and paste it into your terminal.

> **Warning: Using ssl?**
>
> If your Panel is using SSL, then Wings must also use SSL.
>
> See [Creating SSL Certificates](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/ssl/) documentation page for how to create these certificates before continuing.

### Starting Wings

To start Wings, simply run the command below, which will start it in a debug mode.
Once you confirmed that it is running without errors, use `CTRL+C` to terminate the process and daemonize it by following the instructions below.
Depending on your server's internet connection pulling and starting Wings for the first time may take a few minutes.

```sh
sudo wings --debug
```

You may optionally add the `--debug` flag to run Wings in debug mode.

### Daemonizing (using systemd)

Running Wings in the background is a simple task, just make sure that it runs without errors before doing
this. Place the contents below in a file called `wings.service` in the `/etc/systemd/system` directory.

```ini title="/etc/systemd/system/wings.service"
[Unit]
Description=Wings Daemon
After=docker.service
Requires=docker.service
PartOf=docker.service

[Service]
User=root
WorkingDirectory=/etc/pelican
LimitNOFILE=4096
PIDFile=/var/run/wings/daemon.pid
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/wings
Restart=on-failure
StartLimitInterval=180
StartLimitBurst=30
RestartSec=5s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Then, run the commands below to reload systemd and start Wings.

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now wings
```

---

# Advanced Wings Configuration

> Advanced Wings config.yml options: private registries, custom network interfaces, Cloudflare proxy, PID limits, throttles, transfer limits and Podman.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/optional-config/

Wings reads its settings from `config.yml` on each node. This page lists which settings the Panel manages and the advanced options you can change by hand: private registries, network interfaces, the Cloudflare proxy, PID limits, throttles and limits for backups, transfers and installs.

> **Danger**
>
> These are advanced configurations for Wings. You risk breaking Wings and making containers unusable if
> you misconfigure something. Proceed only if you know what each configuration value does.

You must apply all changes to your Wings `config.yml` file located at `/etc/pelican` and restart wings.
Verify your config file using [Yaml Lint](http://www.yamllint.com/) should you receive errors related to YAML parsing.

## Managed by the Panel

Some values are managed by the Panel and appear in the Configuration File tab of the Node.
Most of them are sent to Wings whenever you save a Node, so if you change one of those by hand in `config.yml`, the Panel overwrites it on the next save. Set them in the Panel instead.

The values marked ✗ in the **Sent on save** column are the exception. Wings doesn't accept them from Panel updates or from the auto deploy command, so changing them in the Panel doesn't change them on the node. Update them in `config.yml` by hand, and keep the Panel setting in sync so the two agree.

| Setting Key                   | Where to set it in the Panel                                                         | Sent on save |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :----------: |
| `uuid`, `token_id`, `token`   | Generated by the Panel (Configuration File tab)                                      |      ✓       |
| `api.port`                    | Basic Settings → Port / Listen Port                                                  |      ✓       |
| `api.ssl.enabled`             | Basic Settings → SSL                                                                 |      ✓       |
| `api.ssl.cert`, `api.ssl.key` | Extra Configuration → SSL Certificate (defaults to the Let's Encrypt paths for the node FQDN) |      ✓       |
| `api.upload_limit`            | Advanced Settings → Upload Limit                                                     |      ✓       |
| `system.sftp.bind_port`       | Advanced Settings → SFTP Port                                                        |      ✓       |
| `system.data`                 | Advanced Settings → Daemon Base Directory                                            |      ✗       |
| `allowed_mounts`              | Mounts (see the note below)                                                          |      ✗       |
| `remote`                      | The Panel URL (`APP_URL`). The auto deploy command sets it with `--panel-url`        |      ✗       |

The collapsed **Extra Configuration** section at the bottom of the Advanced Settings tab on the Edit Node page can also set the options marked with ✓ in the **Panel** column of the tables below.
A field left empty in the Panel is not sent, and Wings keeps its own value. Clearing a field in the Panel does **not** reset a value Wings already applied. To reset it, edit `config.yml` by hand.

Options marked with ✗ can only be changed by editing `config.yml` on the node.

> **Info**
>
> Wings doesn't accept `allowed_mounts` from the Panel's config updates, so extra mount paths must be added to `config.yml` by hand. The list in the Configuration File tab only includes the Mounts assigned to the node.

> **Info**
>
> Custom SSL certificate paths are applied when you save the Node. Wings ignores Let's Encrypt paths sent by the Panel and keeps the paths it already has, so clearing a custom path in the Panel won't switch Wings back. Edit `api.ssl.cert` and `api.ssl.key` in `config.yml` to do that.

> **Info**
>
> Wings applies Panel updates by merging them into its current configuration. Options that Wings reads under a different name from the Panel's JSON payload can't be set from the Panel, which is why some options are `config.yml` only.
> If you want Wings to ignore everything the Panel sends, set `ignore_panel_config_updates: true`.

## Private Registries

You can use these settings to authenticate against (private) docker registries when pulling images.

### Available Keys

| Setting Key | Default Value | Panel | Notes             |
| ----------- | :-----------: | :---: | ----------------- |
| name        |     null      |   ✗   | Registry address  |
| username    |     null      |   ✗   | Registry username |
| password    |     null      |   ✗   | Registry password |

### Example of usage

```yml
docker:
  registries:
    registry.example.com:
      username: "registryusername"
      password: "registrypassword"
```

## Custom Network Interfaces

You can change the network interface that Wings uses for all containers by editing the network name; it is by default set to `pelican_nw`. For example, to enable Docker host mode change the network name to `host`.

> **Warning**
>
> Changing network mode to `host` grants Pelican direct access to all machine interfaces and Panel users can bind to any IP or Port even if it's not allocated to their container. You will lose all benefits of Docker network isolation. It is not recommended for public installations that are hosting other users' servers.

### Example of usage

```yml
docker:
  network:
    name: host
    network_mode: host
```

After making changes, the following commands will stop the Wings, remove the Pelican network, and start the Wings again. Run at your own risk.
`systemctl stop wings && docker network rm pelican_nw && systemctl start wings`

### All Docker Network Keys

All of these keys live under `docker.network`.

> **Warning**
>
> Containers use `network_mode`, which can only be set in `config.yml`. If you change `name` (in the Panel or in `config.yml`), set `network_mode` to the same value, then remove the old network and restart Wings as shown above. Otherwise containers keep using the old network mode.

| Setting Key           |     Default Value      | Panel | Notes                                                                              |
| :-------------------- | :--------------------: | :---: | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| name                  |      `pelican_nw`      |   ✓   | Name of the Docker network. It is created if it doesn't exist                      |
| network_mode          |      `pelican_nw`      |   ✗   | Docker network mode for containers, e.g. `host`                                    |
| driver                |        `bridge`        |   ✓   | Docker network driver                                                              |
| interface             |      `172.18.0.1`      |   ✓   | Interface used to create the network. Must not conflict with other Docker networks |
| dns                   |  `1.1.1.1`, `1.0.0.1`  |   ✓   | DNS servers used by containers                                                     |
| ispn                  |        `false`         |   ✓   | Use the ISPN network option                                                        |
| IPv6                  |         `true`         |   ✓   | Enable IPv6 on the network                                                         |
| is_internal           |        `false`         |   ✗   | Create the network as internal, with no outbound access                            |
| enable_icc            |         `true`         |   ✗   | Allow inter-container communication on the network                                 |
| network_mtu           |         `1500`         |   ✗   | MTU of the network                                                                 |
| interfaces.v4.subnet  |    `172.18.0.0/16`     |   ✓   | IPv4 subnet of the network                                                         |
| interfaces.v4.gateway |      `172.18.0.1`      |   ✓   | IPv4 gateway of the network                                                        |
| interfaces.v6.subnet  | `fdba:17c8:6c94::/64`  |   ✓   | IPv6 subnet of the network                                                         |
| interfaces.v6.gateway | `fdba:17c8:6c94::1011` |   ✓   | IPv6 gateway of the network                                                        |

```yml
docker:
  network:
    interface: 172.18.0.1
    dns:
      - 1.1.1.1
      - 1.0.0.1
    name: pelican_nw
    ispn: false
    IPv6: true
    driver: bridge
    network_mode: pelican_nw
    is_internal: false
    enable_icc: true
    network_mtu: 1500
    interfaces:
      v4:
        subnet: 172.18.0.0/16
        gateway: 172.18.0.1
      v6:
        subnet: fdba:17c8:6c94::/64
        gateway: fdba:17c8:6c94::1011
```

## Enabling Cloudflare proxy

Cloudflare proxying of the Wings isn't beneficial since users will be connecting to the machine directly and bypassing any Cloudflare protection. As such, your Node machine IP will still be exposed.

To enable Cloudflare proxy, you must change the Wings port to one of the Cloudflare HTTPS ports with caching enabled (more info [here](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/get-started/reference/network-ports/)), such as 8443, because Cloudflare only supports HTTP on port 8080. Select your Node in the Admin Panel, and on the settings tab, change the port. Make sure that you set "Not Behind Proxy" when using Full SSL settings in Cloudflare. Then on Cloudflare dashboard, your FQDN must have an orange cloud enabled beside it.

You are unable to proxy the SFTP port through Cloudflare unless you have their enterprise plan. Server transfers will most likely not work either due to [Cloudflare's request body limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#request-limits).

## Container PID Limit

You can change the total number of processes that can be active in a container at any given moment by changing the `container_pid_limit` value. The default value is `512`, and it can also be set in the Panel.
You can set it to `0` to disable the limit completely. However, this is _not_ recommended as the limit prevents malicious overloading of the node.
Restart wings and your game server to apply the new limit.

### Example of usage

```yml
docker:
  ...
  container_pid_limit: 512
  ...
```

## Other Docker Settings

All of these keys live under `docker`.

| Setting Key                 | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                                                         |
| :-------------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| domainname                  |     empty     |   ✓   | Docker domain name for all containers                                                                                                         |
| tmpfs_size                  |      100      |   ✓   | Size of the `/tmp` directory in MiB mounted into containers. Docker uses host memory for this, and it isn't counted against the server       |
| userns_mode                 |     empty     |   ✓   | User namespace mode for containers when Docker user namespace remapping is enabled. Set to `host` to disable remapping for Pelican containers |
| system_ips                  |      []       |   ✓   | IP addresses that users are allowed to bind to                                                                                                |
| use_performant_inspect      |     true      |   ✓   | Use a faster container inspect call                                                                                                           |
| overhead.override           |     false     |   ✓   | Use the values below instead of the built-in memory overhead tiers                                                                            |
| overhead.default_multiplier |     1.05      |   ✓   | Memory multiplier given to containers when overriding, so software such as the JVM stays below its limit                                      |
| overhead.multipliers        |     empty     |   ✗   | Map of memory size (MiB) to multiplier, used instead of `default_multiplier` for servers at or below that size                                |
| log_config.type             |    `local`    |   ✓   | Docker log driver for containers                                                                                                              |
| log_config.config           |   see below   |   ✗   | Options passed to the log driver                                                                                                              |

When `overhead.override` is `false`, Wings gives servers with 2048 MiB of memory or less 15% extra, servers with 4096 MiB or less 10% extra, and all other servers 5% extra.

```yml
docker:
  domainname: ""
  tmpfs_size: 100
  userns_mode: ""
  system_ips: []
  use_performant_inspect: true
  overhead:
    override: false
    default_multiplier: 1.05
    multipliers:
      2048: 1.15
      4096: 1.10
  log_config:
    type: local
    config:
      compress: "false"
      max-file: "1"
      max-size: 5m
      mode: non-blocking
```

## Throttles Limits

You can use these settings to adjust or completely disable console throttling.

| Setting Key         | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                      |
| :------------------ | :-----------: | :---: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| enabled             |     true      |   ✓   | Whether or not the throttler is enabled                                                    |
| lines               |     2000      |   ✓   | Total lines that can be output in a given line_reset_interval period                       |
| line_reset_interval |      100      |   ✓   | The amount of time in milliseconds after which the number of lines processed is reset to 0 |

### Example of usage

```yml
throttles:
  enabled: true
  lines: 2000
  line_reset_interval: 100
```

## Backups Limits

These keys live under `system.backups`.

| Setting Key                     | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                                               |
| :------------------------------ | :-----------: | :---: | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| write_limit                     |       0       |   ✗   | Impose I/O write limit for backups to the disk, 0 = unlimited. Value greater than 0 throttles write speed to the set value in MiB/s |
| compression_level               | `best_speed`  |   ✗   | `none` for no compression, `best_speed` for gzip level 1, or `best_compression` for gzip level 9                                    |
| restore_host_allowlist          |      []       |   ✗   | Hostnames, IP addresses or CIDR ranges that backup restores may download from even though they are private or internal             |
| remove_backups_on_server_delete |     true      |   ✗   | Delete a server's local backups when the server is deleted                                                                          |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  backups:
    write_limit: 0
    compression_level: best_speed
    restore_host_allowlist: []
    remove_backups_on_server_delete: true
```

## Transfers Limits

These keys live under `system.transfers`.

| Setting Key            | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                                            |
| :--------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| download_limit         |       0       |   ✗   | Impose a Network I/O read limit for archives, 0 = unlimited. Value greater than 0 throttles read speed to the set value in MiB/s |
| storage_pool.enabled   |     false     |   ✗   | Signals that this node shares a common data volume with other nodes                                                              |
| storage_pool.pool_name |     empty     |   ✗   | Identifier used to check whether two nodes are in the same shared storage pool                                                   |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  transfers:
    download_limit: 0
    storage_pool:
      enabled: false
      pool_name: ""
```

## Installer Limits

Defines the limits on the installer containers that prevents a server's installation process from unintentionally consuming more resources than expected. This is used in conjunction with the server's defined limits. Whichever value is higher will take precedence in the install containers.

| Setting Key | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                       |
| :---------- | :-----------: | :---: | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| memory      |     1024      |   ✓   | The maximum amount of memory install container can use unless server memory limit is higher than this value |
| cpu         |      100      |   ✓   | The maximum amount of cpu install container can use unless server cpu limit is higher than this value       |

### Example of usage

```yml
docker:
  installer_limits:
    memory: 1024
    cpu: 100
```

## Crash Detection

These keys live under `system.crash_detection`, except `crash_detection_activity_lines`, which lives directly under `system`.

| Setting Key                    | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                           |
| :----------------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| enabled                        |     true      |   ✗   | Enable crash detection for all servers on this node                                             |
| detect_clean_exit_as_crash     |     true      |   ✗   | Mark server as crashed if it's stopped without user interaction, e.g., not pressing stop button |
| timeout                        |      60       |   ✗   | Seconds between crashes that won't cause the server to be restarted again. Prevents boot loops  |
| crash_detection_activity_lines |       2       |   ✗   | Number of console lines added to the activity log when a server crashes                         |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  crash_detection:
    enabled: true
    detect_clean_exit_as_crash: true
    timeout: 60
  crash_detection_activity_lines: 2
```

## SFTP

These keys live under `system.sftp`. `bind_port` is managed by the Panel.

| Setting Key  | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                 |
| :----------- | :-----------: | :---: | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| bind_address |   `0.0.0.0`   |   ✓   | Address the SFTP server listens on                    |
| read_only    |     false     |   ✗   | Block all write actions over SFTP                     |
| key_only     |     false     |   ✗   | Only allow SSH key logins, so passwords can't be used |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  sftp:
    bind_address: 0.0.0.0
    bind_port: 2022
    read_only: false
    key_only: false
```

## System Directories

These keys live under `system`. `data` is managed by the Panel.

| Setting Key       |        Default Value        | Panel | Notes                                                                                   |
| :---------------- | :-------------------------: | :---: | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| root_directory    |     `/var/lib/pelican`      |   ✗   | Root directory where all Pelican data is stored                                         |
| log_directory     |     `/var/log/pelican`      |   ✗   | Directory for server installation logs and other Wings logs                             |
| archive_directory | `/var/lib/pelican/archives` |   ✗   | Directory where server transfer archives are stored                                     |
| backup_directory  | `/var/lib/pelican/backups`  |   ✗   | Directory where local backups are stored                                                |
| tmp_directory     |       `/tmp/pelican`        |   ✗   | Directory for temporary files during installs. Useful for docker-in-docker environments |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  root_directory: /var/lib/pelican
  log_directory: /var/log/pelican
  data: /var/lib/pelican/volumes
  archive_directory: /var/lib/pelican/archives
  backup_directory: /var/lib/pelican/backups
  tmp_directory: /tmp/pelican
```

## System User and Rootless Docker

These keys live under `system`.

| Setting Key                 |       Default Value       | Panel | Notes                                                                                        |
| :-------------------------- | :-----------------------: | :---: | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| username                    |         `pelican`         |   ✓   | System user that owns server files and is used inside containers                             |
| timezone                    |       auto-detected       |   ✓   | Timezone passed into all containers. Wings detects it, falling back to `UTC`                 |
| user.uid / user.gid         |       set by Wings        |   ✗   | UID and GID of the system user. Wings fills these in when it boots                           |
| user.rootless.enabled       |           false           |   ✓   | Enable when Docker runs in rootless mode                                                     |
| user.rootless.container_uid |             0             |   ✗   | UID of the user inside the container. Usually `0`, so the container runs as the Wings user   |
| user.rootless.container_gid |             0             |   ✗   | GID of the user inside the container. Usually `0`, so the container runs as the Wings user   |
| user.passwd.enable          |           true            |   ✓   | Mount a generated passwd and group file into containers to fix missing user and group errors |
| user.passwd.directory       |      `/etc/pelican`       |   ✗   | Directory where the passwd and group files are generated                                     |
| machine_id.enable           |           true            |   ✓   | Generate and mount a `machine-id` file into containers. Some games, such as Hytale, need it  |
| machine_id.directory        | `/etc/pelican/machine-id` |   ✗   | Directory where the `machine-id` files are generated                                         |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  username: pelican
  timezone: UTC
  user:
    rootless:
      enabled: false
      container_uid: 0
      container_gid: 0
    passwd:
      enable: true
      directory: /etc/pelican
  machine_id:
    enable: true
    directory: /etc/pelican/machine-id
```

## Disk Usage and Quotas

These keys live under `system`.

| Setting Key         | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                                                                       |
| :------------------ | :-----------: | :---: | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| disk_check_interval |      150      |   ✗   | Seconds before a server's disk usage is recalculated. Low values can cause heavy I/O and CPU load. `0` disables disk checking, so disk usage always shows 0 |
| quotas.enabled      |     false     |   ✓   | Enable quota management on the data directory. See [Disk Quotas](https://pelican.dev/docs/guides/disk-quotas/about/)                                                            |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  disk_check_interval: 150
  quotas:
    enabled: false
```

## Activity and Logging

These keys live under `system`. For container log settings, see `log_config` in [Other Docker Settings](#other-docker-settings).

| Setting Key            | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                    |
| :--------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| activity_send_interval |      60       |   ✗   | Seconds between sending batches of server activity to the Panel          |
| activity_send_count    |      100      |   ✗   | Number of activity events sent per batch                                 |
| websocket_log_count    |      150      |   ✗   | Number of console lines sent when someone connects to a server's console |
| enable_log_rotate      |     true      |   ✗   | Write a logrotate configuration for Wings when it boots and none exists  |

### Example of usage

```yml
system:
  activity_send_interval: 60
  activity_send_count: 100
  websocket_log_count: 150
  enable_log_rotate: true
```

## API

These keys live under `api`. `host`, `port`, `ssl` and `upload_limit` are managed by the Panel.

| Setting Key                   | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                               |
| :---------------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| disable_remote_download       |     false     |   ✗   | Disable downloading files from a URL into server directories        |
| remote_download.max_redirects |      10       |   ✓   | Maximum HTTP redirects followed during a remote download            |
| trusted_proxies               |      []       |   ✓   | IP addresses of proxies allowed to set the `X-Forwarded-For` header |

### Example of usage

```yml
api:
  disable_remote_download: false
  remote_download:
    max_redirects: 10
  trusted_proxies:
    - 10.0.0.1
```

## Panel Connection

These keys live under `remote_query`.

| Setting Key           | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                                |
| :-------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| timeout               |      30       |   ✓   | Seconds Wings waits for a Panel API request before marking it failed                                                 |
| boot_servers_per_page |      50       |   ✗   | Servers requested per page when Wings boots. Raising it isn't recommended, as it can hit memory limits on the Panel |
| custom_headers        |     empty     |   ✗   | Extra headers sent with every request to the Panel, e.g. to get past Cloudflare Access                               |

### Example of usage

```yml
remote_query:
  timeout: 30
  boot_servers_per_page: 50
  custom_headers:
    CF-Access-Client-Id: "client-id"
    CF-Access-Client-Secret: "client-secret"
```

## CORS

| Setting Key                | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                                                                                 |
| :------------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| allowed_origins            |      []       |   ✓   | Extra request origins to allow. The Panel URL is always allowed                                                                                                       |
| allow_cors_private_network |     false     |   ✓   | Sends the `Access-Control-Request-Private-Network` header. Only needed when connecting to Wings over HTTP on an internal IP address. Most users should leave this off |

### Example of usage

```yml
allowed_origins:
  - https://panel.example.com
allow_cors_private_network: false
```

## File Search

These keys live under `Search`. Note the capital `S`.

| Setting Key         |                            Default Value                            | Panel | Notes                                        |
| :------------------ | :-----------------------------------------------------------------: | :---: | -------------------------------------------- |
| blacklisted_dirs    | `node_modules`, `.git`, `.wine`, `appcache`, `depotcache`, `vendor` |   ✗   | Directory names skipped when searching files |
| max_recursion_depth |                                  8                                  |   ✗   | Maximum directory depth searched             |

### Example of usage

```yml
Search:
  blacklisted_dirs:
    - node_modules
    - .git
    - .wine
    - appcache
    - depotcache
    - vendor
  max_recursion_depth: 8
```

## Other values

More commonly discussed values.

| Setting Key                      | Default Value | Panel | Notes                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------- | :-----------: | :---: | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| debug                            |     false     |   ✓   | Force Wings to run in debug mode                                                                                                                           |
| quiet                            |     false     |   ✗   | Run Wings with minimal logging. Ignored in debug mode                                                                                                      |
| app_name                         |   `pelican`   |   ✓   | Application name used by Wings                                                                                                                             |
| system.check_permissions_on_boot |     true      |   ✗   | Check all file permissions on each boot. Disable this when you have a very large amount of files and the server startup is hanging on checking permissions |
| system.openat_mode               |    `auto`     |   ✗   | Controls whether Wings uses the newer `openat2` syscall for server file access. Leave on `auto` unless you are troubleshooting file access issues           |
| BlockBaseDirMount                |     true      |   ✗   | Block mounts that target `/home/container`. Note the capitalization                                                                                        |
| ignore_panel_config_updates      |     false     |   ✗   | Ignore configuration updates sent by the Panel. Values set in the Panel then have no effect on this node                                                   |

### Example of usage

```yml
debug: false
quiet: false
app_name: pelican
system:
  check_permissions_on_boot: true
  openat_mode: auto
BlockBaseDirMount: true
ignore_panel_config_updates: false
```

## Running on Podman

Wings can use rootful Podman in place of Docker through Podman's Docker-compatible API. Wings runs as root, so it uses the system Podman socket. These steps assume a Fedora, RHEL, or Alma/Rocky Linux host with SELinux enforcing.

1. Install Podman's Docker compatibility package and enable the socket. This makes `/var/run/docker.sock` point at Podman, so skip the Docker install step.

    ```sh
    sudo dnf install podman podman-docker policycoreutils-python-utils
    sudo systemctl enable --now podman.socket
    ```

2. Install and configure Wings as described in [Installing Wings](https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/install/), but in `wings.service` replace the three lines that reference `docker.service` with the following, otherwise systemd refuses to start it (`Unit docker.service not found`):

    ```ini title="/etc/systemd/system/wings.service"
    After=podman.socket
    Requires=podman.socket
    ```

3. Podman doesn't support Docker's `local` log driver, so server installs fail with `invalid log driver`. Wings also mounts its temporary directory into install containers, and SELinux blocks containers from reading `/tmp/pelican`. In `/etc/pelican/config.yml`, change these two values:

    ```yaml title="/etc/pelican/config.yml"
    system:
      tmp_directory: /var/lib/pelican/tmp
    docker:
      log_config:
        type: k8s-file
    ```

4. Allow containers to use the Wings data directories under SELinux, then restart Wings:

    ```sh
    sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/pelican/tmp
    sudo semanage fcontext -a -t container_file_t "/var/lib/pelican(/.*)?"
    sudo restorecon -R /var/lib/pelican
    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
    sudo systemctl restart wings
    ```

> **Warning**
>
> Keep the OOM killer enabled on every server. Podman uses cgroup v2, which can't disable it, so a server with the OOM killer disabled fails to install or start with `cannot disable OOM killer with cgroupv2`.

---

# Updating Wings

> Update Wings with the built-in self-updater or by replacing the binary manually, then restart the service. Running servers are not affected.

Source: https://pelican.dev/docs/wings/update/

Updating Wings is a painless process and should take less than a minute to complete.

## Wings Version Requirements

| Panel Version | Wings Version | Supported |
|:-------------:|:-------------:|:---------:|
|      1.x      |      1.x      |    ✅︎     |

## Download Update

> **Tip**
>
> Running servers **will not** be affected.

### Self-update

First, run the Wings auto-updater.

```sh
sudo wings update
```

### Manual update

First, download the updated wings binary into `/usr/local/bin`. You will need to stop Wings briefly.

```sh
sudo systemctl stop wings
sudo curl -L -o /usr/local/bin/wings "https://github.com/pelican/wings/releases/latest/download/wings_linux_$([[ "$(uname -m)" == "x86_64" ]] && echo "amd64" || echo "arm64")"
sudo chmod u+x /usr/local/bin/wings
```

## Restart

Secondly, Restart the process.

```sh
sudo systemctl restart wings
```
